---
URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/mimo-elm-energy-mix.html
Title: MIMO-ELM: forecasting every source of an island electricity grid at once
Language: en
Description: Multi-input multi-output extreme learning machines for the Corsican electricity mix: why forecast all sources together, SISO vs MIMO vs MIMO-MH…

Solar forecasting explained · 22 October 2026 · Published article (MIMO) and manuscript, submission in progress (MIMO-MH) · open code and data
MIMO-ELM: forecasting every source of an island electricity grid at once
Principle 4 · Every tool, at the peripheryThe approachIn the story: when no equation links the sources, let the machine learn, simply, parsimoniously, frugally: one ELM forecasts seven grid signals at once (nRMSE 0.179 for solar, 0.051 for thermal, one hour ahead).
In brief
One extreme learning machine forecasts the seven signals of the Corsican electricity grid at once (total, thermal, imports, hydropower, solar, wind, bioenergy) from the last 48 hours.
One hour ahead, the published study reports a normalized RMSE (nRMSE) of 0.179 for solar and 0.051 for thermal, with a coefficient of determination R² above 0.98, ahead of persistence and of an LSTM (long short-term memory network) tuned with a realistic budget.
Published in Applied Energy 410, 127599 (2026) by C. Voyant, M. Despotovic, L. Garcia-Gutierrez, M. Asloune, Y.-M. Saint-Drenan, J.-L. Duchaud, G. A. Faggianelli and E. Magliaro; MATLAB and Python code with EDF open data, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23562559.
On an island grid, production must match consumption at every moment. The operator needs forecasts of every source and of the total, and they must add up. One model that predicts all of them together can be more coherent, and with an extreme learning machine it trains in seconds.
The question
Corsica's electricity comes from thermal plants, imports through the interconnections, hydropower, solar, wind and bioenergy. The sources are not independent: when solar rises at noon, thermal and imports adjust. Forecasting each source separately ignores these links and gives forecasts whose sum need not equal the forecast total.
A week of July 2022 (EDF Corse open data). Solar covers the middle of the day; thermal and imports follow the evening demand. PDF
Three ways to organize the models
SISO: one model per source and per horizon, each reading only the history of its own source.
MIMO (the published article): one model per horizon reads the last 48 hours of all sources, plus the hour of the day, and predicts all of them at once.
MIMO-MH (the manuscript in submission): a single model predicts all sources for all horizons from 1 to 24 hours, followed by a reconciliation step that makes the forecasts add up.
What one trained model predicts in each organization. PDF
The theory
Why, in the words of the article: on an island grid the energy sources balance one another (when one varies, the others adjust), so predicting each source and their sum with the same algorithm lets these balancing effects enter the learning, potentially giving a better forecast of the residual demand than one model per source. Six years of hourly data from Corsica (solar, wind, hydropower, thermal, bioenergy and imports, plus the total) are forecast with an extreme learning machine in a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architecture. Equation numbers are those of the article (arXiv:2508.12764).
Why several outputs: the mutual information (Eqs. 1 and 2)
$$\mathrm{MI}(X;Y)=\iint p(x,y)\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)\,p(y)}\,dx\,dy\ \ (1),$$
$$\mathrm{MI}_{\mathrm{norm}}(X;Y)=\frac{\mathrm{MI}(X;Y)}{\sqrt{H(X)\,H(Y)}}\in[0,1]\ \ (2).$$
Here \(p\) denotes probability densities and \(H\) entropy. Unlike the Pearson correlation, the normalized mutual information captures non-linear dependencies. Thermal and bioenergy (0.535), solar and bioenergy (0.468), hydropower and thermal (0.373) are strongly linked; the total depends mainly on thermal (0.256), imports (0.231), hydropower (0.129) and solar (0.124). These links support a MIMO approach.
Inputs and outputs
Sliding window
the last \(w\) hours of all seven signals; \(w\) chosen by exhaustive search from 24 to 96 hours with 212 hidden nodes: \(w=48\) is best
Time encoding
\(\sin(2\pi t/24)\) and \(\cos(2\pi t/24)\), with \(t\) the hour of the day
Inputs, outputs
\(7\times48+2\) inputs; 7 outputs, the seven signals at the forecast horizon
Reference
persistence, \(\hat y_{t+h}=y_t\)
The extreme learning machine of the article
For an input vector \(\mathbf x\), hidden neuron \(j\) computes a ReLU of a random projection, and the output is linear in the hidden layer:
$$h_j(\mathbf x)=\max\!\big(0,\ \mathbf w_j^{\top}\mathbf x+b_j\big),$$
$$\mathbf y=H^{\top}W,$$
$$W=H^{+}Y,$$
with \(H\) the hidden-layer outputs, \(Y\) the targets, \(W\) the output weights and \(H^{+}\) the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse: the input weights and biases are drawn at random and never trained, and the output weights minimize the mean squared error over all outputs in one closed-form step. Fifty random initializations are drawn and the best one, by in-sample RMSE, is kept. With 4,096 hidden neurons the model has 1,413,120 parameters and trains in 104.1 s per initialization on a laptop; the LSTM of the comparison (500 hidden neurons, 1,023,507 parameters) needs 2,651.6 s, about 25 times longer, and an LSTM with 4,096 neurons was infeasible on the same machine. Being closed-form, the ELM can be retrained continuously on a sliding window (online learning).
What the article shows
The ELM significantly outperforms persistence, particularly for solar and thermal production: nRMSE 17.9 % and 5.1 % with R² > 0.98 one hour ahead. Accuracy stays high up to five hours ahead, beyond which renewable sources become increasingly volatile. MIMO gives marginal gains over single-output (SISO) models and, against the LSTM, a closed-form solution at a much lower computational cost, suited to real-time use.
Beyond the article: forecasts that add up (MIMO-MH, manuscript in submission)
The article mentions reconciliation as another strategy for linked quantities. The repository adds, for the multi-horizon extension under submission, a weighted least-squares reconciliation that makes the forecast total equal the sum of the sources: with the summing matrix \(S\) and the error variances \(W\),
$$\tilde{\mathbf y}=S\left(S^{\top}W^{-1}S\right)^{-1}S^{\top}W^{-1}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
No result of that manuscript is reported here.
Worked example: making forecasts add up
For one hour, suppose the forecasts are 330 MW for the total, 150 for thermal, 90 for imports and 80 for solar, with error variances 36, 25, 49 and 100 MW². The components sum to 320, not 330. Weighted least-squares reconciliation finds the coherent forecasts closest to the original ones, trusting the more reliable forecasts more: thermal 151.2, imports 92.3, solar 84.8 and total 328.3 MW. The gap is closed; solar, the least reliable, moves most. Illustrative values; the formula and its use are in the repository.
Run it
The worked example above, computed with the formula of the theory section (Python 3, NumPy; executed on 22 October 2026). The full pipeline: main in MATLAB for MIMO-ELM, cd mimo_mh && python main.py for SISO, MIMO, MIMO-MH and reconciliation (mimo_mh/reconciliation.py).
import numpy as np
y_hat = np.array([330.0, 150.0, 90.0, 80.0]) # total, thermal, imports, solar (MW)
W = np.diag([36.0, 25.0, 49.0, 100.0]) # error variances (MW^2)
S = np.vstack([np.ones(3), np.eye(3)]) # total = sum of the three sources
Wi = np.linalg.inv(W)
y_tilde = S @ np.linalg.solve(S.T @ Wi @ S, S.T @ Wi @ y_hat)
print(y_tilde.round(1))
Output:
[328.3 151.2 92.3 84.8]
Results of the published article
From its abstract: one hour ahead, solar and thermal production are forecast with nRMSE 0.179 and 0.051 and R² above 0.98; total demand stays reliable up to five hours ahead; wind and bioenergy remain hard; MIMO-ELM improves on persistence and on an LSTM tuned with a realistic budget, with small but stable gains over SISO. The MIMO-MH results will be reported with its article.
Code and data
One repository gathers the MATLAB code of the article (MIMO-ELM, SISO and LSTM comparisons), the Python pipeline of MIMO-MH with reconciliation (written by Yoan Jheelan), and the hourly EDF Corse data 2016–2022, released under the Licence Ouverte.
main % MATLAB: MIMO-ELM with the settings of the article
cd mimo_mh && python main.py % Python: SISO, MIMO, MIMO-MH, reconciliation

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/nice-metrics-fr.html
Title: Métriques NICEᵏ : évaluer une prévision solaire face à la persistance
Language: fr
Other language: en: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/nice-metrics.html
Description: Guide français des métriques NICEᵏ : persistance, normes d’erreur, équations, interprétation, limites, exemple MATLAB et calculateur interactif.

Prévision solaire expliquée · Article publié · Code ouvert
Métriques NICEᵏ : évaluer une prévision solaire face à la persistance
Les métriques NICEᵏ ont été introduites par Voyant et al. dans Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments (2025).
Principe 5 · Démontrer la confiance Voir l’approcheUne erreur n’a de sens qu’avec une référence, un horizon et les observations évaluées.
En bref
NICEᵏ compare une prévision déterministe à la persistance simple : répéter la dernière observation connue. Les deux erreurs sont calculées aux mêmes dates cibles.
NICE¹ utilise la MAE (erreur absolue moyenne), NICE² la RMSE (racine de l’erreur quadratique moyenne) et NICE³ la racine de l’erreur cubique moyenne. NICEΣ combine ces trois rapports ; le cas équilibré emploie trois poids égaux.
L’échelle utile de NICE va de 0 à 1 : 0 pour une prévision parfaite, 1 pour la persistance simple. Un modèle retenu pour son gain sur cette référence doit rester sous 1 pour la norme considérée.
Ce que NICE ajoute
La RMSE dépend de l’échelle du signal ; la MAE donne moins de poids aux grands écarts. Une comparaison relative devient difficile si chaque étude choisit une référence différente. L’équipe de l’article fixe une référence explicite, la persistance simple, puis compare trois normes d’erreur. La référence et le modèle doivent toujours être évalués sur le même ensemble d’observations.
Les figures suivantes illustrent une démonstration synthétique du dépôt NICE. Elles ne remplacent pas l’évaluation sur les données des 68 stations SIAR étudiées dans l’article.
Signal synthétique sur trois jours. La persistance simple reprend la dernière observation et se décale d’une heure. La persistance intelligente corrige ce décalage avec la forme du ciel clair ; AR(1) utilise aussi la corrélation du résidu.
Scores de la même démonstration. La ligne à 1 est la persistance simple ; 0 correspondrait à une prévision parfaite. Figure redessinée à partir de results/demo_scores.csv, pour la persistance intelligente et AR(1) seulement.
Questions fréquentes
Que mesure NICEᵏ ?
La norme d’erreur d’un modèle divisée par celle de la persistance simple au même horizon, sur les mêmes dates cibles. NICE mesure un gain relatif sur une évaluation déterministe, pas la valeur opérationnelle complète d’un modèle.
Que signifie une valeur de 0,8 ?
La norme considérée est 20 % plus faible que celle de la persistance sur cet échantillon. Ce pourcentage ne vaut pas pour toutes les autres normes, tous les sites ou tous les usages économiques.
Et si le quotient brut sort de cette échelle ?
Un résultat > 1 signale que le modèle est moins bon que la persistance sur la norme considérée : il est hors de l’échelle utile 0–1 présentée par l’article. Le code la conserve pour rendre cet échec visible. Si l’erreur de persistance vaut zéro, le quotient est indéfini.
La méthode et ses équations
Les formules reprennent la définition empirique de l’article. Pour éviter une collision de notation, N désigne ici le nombre de cibles évaluées et h l’horizon en pas de temps. À chaque cible j, le modèle propose une valeur et la persistance reprend l’observation disponible h pas plus tôt.
Une seule référence pour les trois normes
$$\hat y_{P,j}=y_{j-h},\qquad E_k(X)=\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|y_j-\hat y_{X,j}|^k\right)^{1/k}.$$
Avec les mêmes dates cibles et le même masque de valeurs valides pour le modèle et la référence :
$$\mathrm{NICE}^{k}=\frac{E_k(X)}{E_k(P)},\qquad k\in\{1,2,3\},\quad E_k(P)>0.$$
NICE¹ rapporte les MAE ; NICE² rapporte les RMSE ; NICE³ rapporte les racines des erreurs cubiques moyennes. L’article part de la RMSE, impose 0 pour une prévision parfaite et 1 pour la persistance, puis généralise aux normes Lk. Les grands écarts pèsent davantage quand k augmente ; au-delà de 3, ils peuvent dominer l’interprétation.
Associer les trois lectures
$$\mathrm{NICE}^{\Sigma}=w_1\mathrm{NICE}^{1}+w_2\mathrm{NICE}^{2}+w_3\mathrm{NICE}^{3},\qquad w_i\geq0,\quad \sum_i w_i=1.$$
Dans le cas équilibré de l’article et du calculateur, w₁ = w₂ = w₃ = 1/3. Une application sensible aux grandes erreurs peut choisir un autre poids pour NICE³ ; ces poids doivent être annoncés.
Pourquoi la persistance dépend du signal
Pour une série faiblement stationnaire de variance σ² et d’autocorrélation ρ(h), l’erreur quadratique moyenne théorique de la persistance suit :
$$\mathbb E\!\left[(y_j-y_{j-h})^2\right]=2\sigma^2\left(1-\rho(h)\right).$$
Une forte autocorrélation réduit l’erreur de persistance et rend cette référence plus difficile à dépasser. Cette relation suppose la stationnarité faible ; l’article juge le rapport empirique d’erreurs le plus utile sur les données étudiées. Les dérivations théoriques de NICE¹ et NICE³ ajoutent une hypothèse de normalité.
Lire et rapporter le résultat
Afficher aussi les MAE, RMSE et erreurs cubiques en unités physiques : le rapport seul ne donne pas la taille des écarts.
Préciser horizon, pas de temps, dates cibles, persistance choisie, valeurs manquantes et éventuel masque nocturne.
Une valeur inférieure à 1 ne prouve ni l’intérêt économique du modèle ni sa supériorité à toutes les autres références possibles.
Essayer le calculateur
Garder la démonstration ou coller deux colonnes alignées : observations et prévisions. Choisir l’horizon en pas de temps. Le calculateur affiche NICE¹, NICE², NICE³ et NICEΣ face à la persistance simple aux mêmes dates cibles.
Reproduire un exemple
Quatre observations horaires, quatre prévisions et la persistance issue de l’heure précédente. L’exemple du README passe explicitement la référence à la fonction pour montrer l’alignement.
y = [500 450 600 550]; % observations (W/m²)
y_hat = [460 480 560 580]; % prévisions du modèle
y_P = [400 500 450 600]; % dernières observations disponibles
m = nice_metrics(y, y_hat, y_P);
fprintf('NICE1 %.3f NICE2 %.3f NICE3 %.3f NICE_Sigma %.3f\n', ...
m.NICE1, m.NICE2, m.NICE3, m.NICE_Sigma);
Valeurs attendues pour cet exemple : NICE¹ = 0,400 ; NICE² = 0,365 ; NICE³ = 0,340 ; NICEΣ = 0,368. Le modèle évite ici surtout le grand écart de persistance, d’où une baisse plus marquée pour la norme cubique. Le dépôt fournit aussi demo_nice.m, ses figures et les scripts de l’article dans paper_scripts/.
Article, équipe et code
Article publié : Cyril Voyant, Milan Despotovic, Luis Garcia-Gutierrez, Rodrigo Amaro e Silva, Philippe Lauret, Ted Soubdhan et Nadjem Bailek, « NICEᵏ metrics: Unified and multidimensional framework for evaluating deterministic solar forecasting accuracy », Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments, vol. 83, article 104588, 2025, doi:10.1016/j.seta.2025.104588 · BibTeX. La méthode et la publication sont le travail de cette équipe ; Cyril Voyant signe cette page de présentation.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/nice-metrics.html
Title: NICEᵏ metrics: solar forecast errors compared with persistence
Language: en
Other language: fr: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/nice-metrics-fr.html
Description: NICEᵏ metrics for deterministic solar forecasting: formula, persistence baseline, meaning of values below one, implementation and the published paper.

Solar forecasting explained · Published article, open code
NICEᵏ metrics: solar forecast errors compared with persistence
The NICEᵏ metrics were introduced by Voyant et al. in Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments (2025).
Principle 5 · Trust is demonstratedThe approachIn the story: measure what a model adds. NICE divides a model's error by that of persistence, so 1 means no gain at all.
In brief
NICEᵏ divides the Lᵏ error of a forecast by that of simple persistence, the forecast that repeats the last observed value, on the same samples: a normalized ratio. A useful forecast lies between 0 (perfect) and 1 (simple persistence); > 1 means worse than simple persistence.
Orders k = 1, 2 and 3 (mean absolute error MAE, root mean square error RMSE, root mean cubic error RMCE) weigh large errors more and more; NICE^Σ combines them with equal weights. Unlike skill scores, NICE does not depend on an arbitrary baseline, and it is linked to the autocorrelation of the series: the more persistent the series, the harder persistence is to beat.
Published in Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments (2025) by C. Voyant, M. Despotovic, L. Garcia-Gutierrez, R. Amaro e Silva, P. Lauret, T. Soubdhan and N. Bailek; MATLAB code with a worked example, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23562549.
What does NICE add?
The study compares the errors of a deterministic forecast with those of simple persistence on the same observations, for three error norms (NICE¹ with the MAE, NICE² with the RMSE, NICE³ with the RMCE) and their weighted combination NICE^Σ (equal weights in the balanced case).
Figure 1 of the nice-metrics repository: three days of a synthetic signal. Simple persistence (dashed red), the reference of NICE, lags the observation by one hour; smart persistence corrects that lag with the clear-sky shape, and the AR(1) model on the clear-sky residual also uses the correlation of the noise.
Scores of the same demonstration: NICEᵏ of smart persistence and of the AR(1) model relative to simple persistence (dashed line at 1; 0 would be a perfect forecast). Redrawn from results/demo_scores.csv of the nice-metrics repository, with smart persistence and AR(1) only.
Cyril Voyant · Updated 2026-10-20
The NICEᵏ metrics (Normalized Informed Comparison of Errors), introduced by Cyril Voyant and co-authors in Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments (2025, doi:10.1016/j.seta.2025.104588 · BibTeX), score a deterministic solar forecast against simple persistence, as an error ratio. A useful forecast lies between 0 (perfect) and 1 (simple persistence); > 1 means worse than simple persistence.
Questions about NICEᵏ solar forecast metrics
What do NICE metrics measure in deterministic solar forecasting?
NICEᵏ compares a forecast error norm with the error norm of a specified persistence forecast on the same observations. It is a reference-relative measure of deterministic forecast accuracy. Here, NICEᵏ refers to the solar forecasting framework published by Voyant and coauthors in 2025, with DOI 10.1016/j.seta.2025.104588 · BibTeX.
What does a NICE component below one mean in solar forecasting?
For the component defined as the ratio of L-k error norms, a value below one means smaller errors than the chosen persistence baseline. A value of 0.8 means that this error norm is 20% smaller on the evaluated samples. It does not imply a 20% improvement in every error metric or in economic value. A zero baseline norm makes the ratio undefined.
The theory
Why a new metric, in the words of the article: the RMSE is scale-dependent, the MAE lacks sensitivity to large deviations, and skill scores depend on arbitrary baselines. NICE (Normalized Informed Comparison of Errors) measures a model against one fixed reference, simple persistence, the forecast that repeats the last observed value, and gives a normalized error ratio whose reference and evaluation samples must be specified. A result > 1 stays visible: the model is worse than simple persistence. The equation numbers below are those of the article.
Definitions
\(y(t)\)
observation at time \(t\), time step \(\Delta t\)
\(\hat y(t)\)
forecast of model X
P
simple persistence: \(\hat y(t)=y(t-\Delta t)\); at horizon \(n\), \(\hat y(t+n\Delta t)=y(t)\). It is the only reference of NICE.
\(n\)
number of evaluated samples, the same for X and P
From the RMSE to NICE² (Eqs. 1 to 4)
$$\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n}\big(y(t)-\hat y(t)\big)^2}\ \ (1),$$
$$\mathrm{RMSE}_P=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n}\big(y(t)-y(t-\Delta t)\big)^2}\ \ (2).$$
Start from \(\mathrm{NICE}^2=\alpha\,\mathrm{RMSE}_X\) (3) and require a perfect forecast to give 0 and persistence to give 1: \(\alpha\,\mathrm{RMSE}_P=1\), so \(\alpha=1/\mathrm{RMSE}_P\) and
$$\mathrm{NICE}^2=\frac{\mathrm{RMSE}_X}{\mathrm{RMSE}_P},$$
$$(4).$$
Generalization to \(L^k\) (Eqs. 5 and 6)
$$\mathrm{NICE}^k=\frac{L^k\text{-Error}_X}{L^k\text{-Error}_P}\ \ (5),$$
$$L^k\text{-Error}=\left(\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n}\big|y(t)-\hat y(t)\big|^{k}\right)^{1/k}\ \ (6).$$
\(k=1\) gives the MAE and treats all errors alike (robust to outliers); \(k=2\) the RMSE, which weighs large deviations more; \(k=3\) the root mean cubic error (RMCE), which amplifies rare large errors (grid management, extreme events). Beyond 3 the metric is dominated by extreme errors and loses interpretability. NICE² is the standard choice; NICE¹ when robustness to outliers matters.
Link with the autocorrelation (Eqs. 7 to 14)
For a weakly stationary series of variance \(\sigma^2\) and lag-\(n\) autocorrelation \(\rho(n)\):
$$E\big[(y(t)-y(t-\Delta t))^2\big]=2\sigma^2\big(1-\rho(1)\big)\ \ (7),$$
$$\mathrm{RMSE}_P\approx\sqrt{2\sigma^2\big(1-\rho(1)\big)}\ \ (8),$$
$$\mathrm{NICE}^2\approx\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt2}\,\frac{\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum_{t}\big(y(t)-\hat y(t)\big)^2}}{\sqrt{1-\rho(1)}}\ \ (9).$$
At horizon \(n\), persistence predicts \(\hat y(t+n\Delta t)=y(t)\), \(E\big[(y(t+n\Delta t)-y(t))^2\big]=2\sigma^2(1-\rho(n))\) (12), and \(\rho(1)\) is replaced by \(\rho(n)\) in (9), which gives Eq. (14). The more autocorrelated the series, the harder persistence is to beat: NICE measures a model against the forecastability of the series. NICE¹ and NICE³ follow the same way under an additional normality assumption (Eq. 10, Appendix B).
NICEΣ (Eqs. 15 to 17)
$$\mathrm{NICE}^{\Sigma}=w_1\mathrm{NICE}^1+w_2\mathrm{NICE}^2+w_3\mathrm{NICE}^3,$$
$$w_1+w_2+w_3=1,\ w_i\ge0\ \ (15,16);$$
the article uses equal weights, \(w_i=1/3\) (17), to stay neutral; a risk-sensitive application can weigh NICE³ more.
How to read it
A useful forecast lies between 0 and 1: 0 is a perfect forecast; 1 is simple persistence; > 1 means worse than simple persistence. A zero reference error makes the ratio undefined. Never clip the ratio to 1.
A value close to 0: the model captures much more of the dynamics than persistence. A value close to 1: it hardly does better than repeating the last value.
A model worse than simple persistence is possible in theory, but in practice its usefulness is highly questionable, and little insight can be gained from evaluating it.
Assumptions and validity
The model and simple persistence are scored on the same samples, horizon and time step. The theoretical forms (8) to (14) assume weak stationarity, reasonable for irradiance at short lags (under one hour) or at daily scale, not for long horizons; the article finds the empirical form (5) the most insightful. The perfect forecast of the lower bound is unattainable in practice. The repository README adds a note on the constant of Eq. (B.5), checked on the arXiv version of the article.
Try it in your browser
Paste an observation and a forecast column, or keep the demo data, give the forecast horizon, and read NICE¹, NICE², NICE³ and NICE-Σ against simple persistence (Eqs. 5, 6, 11 and 17 of the article).
Run it
The model keeps about a third of the error of simple persistence. NICE³ is the lowest because the model removes the 150 W/m² miss that dominates the cubic error of persistence. Called as nice_metrics(y, y_hat) on a regularly sampled series, the reference is simple persistence y(t-1). Executed with MATLAB R2025b on 23 October 2026.
% from a clone of github.com/cyrilvoyant/nice-metrics: the worked example of the README
y = [500 450 600 550]; % observed irradiance, hours 2 to 5 (W/m2)
y_hat = [460 480 560 580]; % model forecast
y_P = [400 500 450 600]; % simple persistence: the observation of the previous hour
m = nice_metrics(y, y_hat, y_P);
fprintf('NICE1 %.3f NICE2 %.3f NICE3 %.3f NICE_Sigma %.3f\n', m.NICE1, m.NICE2, m.NICE3, m.NICE_Sigma);
Output:
NICE1 0.400 NICE2 0.365 NICE3 0.340 NICE_Sigma 0.368
The repository also contains demo_nice.m (teaching demonstration with figures) and the article's own scripts, unchanged, in paper_scripts/.
Reporting protocol
State persistence definition, horizon, temporal alignment, scoring window and missing-value mask. Report absolute errors alongside the ratio. A ratio below one does not establish operational value or superiority to every possible baseline.
Reference and implementation
NICEᵏ Metrics: Unified and Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Deterministic Solar Forecasting Accuracy, 2025. Credit all authors as listed in the publication. The nice-metrics repository (archived: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23562549) gives the MATLAB functions, a worked example by hand, a teaching demonstration with figures and the article's scripts; the PV_ELM_pred repository uses the metrics in a full benchmark. See PV forecasting protocol.
Publication authors: Cyril Voyant, Milan Despotovic, Luis Garcia-Gutierrez, Rodrigo Amaro e Silva, Philippe Lauret, Ted Soubdhan, Nadjem Bailek.
Related: persistence and BLEND · γ-index for displaced forecasts · PV_ELM_pred benchmark · deseasonalization benchmark.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/persistence-blend-fr.html
Title: BLEND et CLIPER : des références de persistance cyclostationnaire
Language: fr
Other language: en: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/persistence-blend.html
Description: Comprendre BLEND et CLIPER : équations de persistance cyclostationnaire, résultats publiés, code MATLAB corrigé, tableaux et limites.

Prévision solaire expliquée · Article publié · Code ouvert v1.1.1
BLEND et CLIPER : des références de persistance cyclostationnaire
BLEND a été introduit par Voyant et al. dans Applied Mathematical Modelling (2026).
Avant de complexifier un modèle, comparer sa prévision à une référence adaptée au rythme de la série. BLEND est une combinaison convexe de la persistance (la dernière mesure) et de la persistance cyclique (la mesure de même phase au cycle précédent).
Dans le fil : ne monter en complexité que si le gain est démontré. Une persistance tenant compte du cycle est un échelon de référence pour juger un modèle entraîné. Voir l’approche.
En bref
Pour une série de période T, BLEND est une combinaison convexe de la persistance simple I(t) et la persistance cyclique I(t−T+nΔt). Dans sa forme simplifiée, le poids de la dernière mesure vaut \(\tilde\lambda=\tfrac12(1+\rho(t,n\Delta t))\).
La référence exploite les moyennes, variances et covariances périodiques. Elle n’entraîne pas de réseau et peut se calculer sur le signal brut, sans modèle de ciel clair.
L’article de Voyant, Banes, Garcia-Gutierrez, Notton, Despotovic et Yaseen, publié dans Applied Mathematical Modelling 157 (2026), 116988, étudie notamment 68 stations espagnoles SIAR. Le code MATLAB corrigé est disponible en version 1.1.1.
Pourquoi BLEND ?
Une série solaire change au fil de la journée : ses moyenne, variance et corrélation dépendent de l’heure, tout en se répétant avec le cycle. Répéter seulement la dernière observation ignore cette organisation. Répéter seulement la valeur d’hier à la même heure ignore les changements récents. BLEND dose ces deux mémoires par un poids dont l’article dérive la valeur optimale en erreur quadratique moyenne, puis une limite analytique simple.
Figure 6 de la version auteur de Voyant et al., Applied Mathematical Modelling (2026) : nRMSE et nMAE moyennes sur 68 stations SIAR. Il s’agit des résultats de l’article, distincts des essais du dépôt v1.1.1 ci-dessous.
Deux questions fréquentes
Pourquoi comparer à la persistance ?
À court horizon, une référence simple peut être difficile à battre. Un modèle n’a pas démontré de gain s’il ne la dépasse pas aux mêmes dates et horizons. Il faut préciser la référence : persistance simple, « smart » normalisée par le ciel clair ou cyclostationnaire. Les métriques NICE quantifient ce rapport d’erreurs.
La persistance cyclostationnaire apprend-elle ?
Elle n’entraîne pas de réseau. Elle exige pourtant des observations passées pour estimer les statistiques du cycle et, selon la variante, son poids. « Sans apprentissage » ne veut pas dire « sans données ».
Le principe mathématique
Statistiques qui se répètent avec le cycle
Pour un processus \(I(t)\) de période \(T\), la moyenne \(\mu(t)\), la variance \(\sigma^2(t)\) et la covariance \(C(t,n\Delta t)\) se répètent après une période. L’autocorrélation locale \(\rho(t,n\Delta t)\) dépend de la phase. Ici \(I(t)\) est la série, \(\Delta t\) son pas de temps, \(n\) l’horizon en pas, \(T\) la période. Les instants \(t\) et \(t-T\) correspondent à la même phase, sans représenter la même observation.
Des références à distinguer
Persistance simple : \(\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=I(t)\).
Persistance cyclique : \(\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=I(t-T+n\Delta t)\) : la valeur observée à la phase visée, au cycle précédent.
Persistance « smart » : \(\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=\frac{I(t)}{I_{\mathrm{ref}}(t)}I_{\mathrm{ref}}(t+n\Delta t)\), avec une référence telle que le ciel clair.
CLIPER : une combinaison convexe de la persistance (la dernière valeur) et de la moyenne. En régime stationnaire, le poids de la moyenne est \(1-\rho(n\Delta t)\) ; la définition 5 de l’article le généralise aux moyennes, variances et corrélations périodiques. La forme cyclostationnaire pondère \(\mu(t)\) et \(I(t)\) ; dans l’article, $$\lambda^{\circlearrowleft}_{\mathrm{CLIPER}}=\frac{[\mu(t+n\Delta t)-\mu(t)]^2+\sigma^2(t)-\rho(t,n\Delta t)\sigma(t)\sigma(t+n\Delta t)}{[\mu(t+n\Delta t)-\mu(t)]^2+\sigma^2(t)}.$$
BLEND : quelle valeur donne-t-on à la dernière mesure ?
Dans toutes les variantes, \(\lambda\) multiplie la dernière valeur, et \(1-\lambda\) la valeur de même phase au cycle précédent :
$$\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=(1-\lambda)I(t-T+n\Delta t)+\lambda I(t).$$
La définition 6 donne le poids optimal lorsque les statistiques sont stationnaires :
$$\lambda_{\mathrm{BLEND}}=\frac{\rho(T)-\rho(n\Delta t)+\rho(n\Delta t-T)-1}{2\bigl(\rho(n\Delta t-T)-1\bigr)}.$$
La définition 7 laisse ce poids varier selon la phase ; son équation (2) incorpore les moyennes, les écarts types et les corrélations cycliques. La formule ci-dessous suit la version imprimée ; le code corrigé documente une différence à cette équation. Pour interpréter et reproduire les résultats, il faut lire ensemble la publication et le README du code v1.1.1.
$$D=(\mu(t)-\mu(t+n\Delta t))^2+\sigma^2(t)+\sigma^2(t+n\Delta t),$$
$$\lambda^{\circlearrowleft}_{\mathrm{BLEND}}=\frac{(\mu(t)-\mu(t+n\Delta t))^2+\sigma^2(t+n\Delta t)[1-\rho(t+n\Delta t,T)]}{D}+\frac{\sigma(t)\sigma(t+n\Delta t)[\rho(t,n\Delta t)-\rho(t,n\Delta t-T)]}{D+2\rho(t,n\Delta t-T)\sigma(t)\sigma(t+n\Delta t)}.$$
La définition 8 fournit la limite analytique centrale :
$$\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{BLEND}}^{\circlearrowleft}=\tfrac12\bigl(1+\rho(t,n\Delta t)\bigr).$$
Une forte corrélation favorise la mesure récente ; une corrélation faible ou négative donne plus de poids au cycle précédent. Cette simplification suppose des moyennes et variances égales aux deux phases comparées, une symétrie de corrélation et une corrélation de long retard négligeable (remarque 17). Quand le dénominateur de la forme générale devient instable, l’article propose de borner doucement \(\lambda\) entre 0 et 1 (remarque 16). La combinaison reste alors compris entre les deux observations utilisées.
Ce que montre l’article
Les auteurs examinent des séries synthétiques cyclostationnaires et l’éclairement à pas de 30 minutes de 68 stations SIAR espagnoles, de 2017 à 2020, à des horizons de 30 minutes à six heures. Les ajustements cyclostationnaires réduisent les erreurs face à leurs équivalents naïfs, surtout aux horizons de plusieurs heures. Sur les séries mesurées, le BLEND simplifié offre un compromis pratique sans normalisation par ciel clair ; les différences sont examinées par tests de Wilcoxon (\(p<0{,}01\)). Cette conclusion porte sur ces jeux de données et ces références.
Explorer dans le navigateur
Conservez la démonstration, collez une série périodique ou chargez l’exemple photovoltaïque public de Palaiseau : vous pouvez voir trois journées entières, régler \(\lambda\) sur la parabole d’erreur d’une phase et comparer BLEND aux persistances simple et cyclique à plusieurs horizons. Le calculateur sert à explorer les poids et les erreurs sur la série fournie. Les résultats hors échantillon sont présentés séparément ci-dessous, avec leur protocole d’apprentissage et de test.
Reproduire avec MATLAB
La version 1.1.1 exige MATLAB R2021a ou plus récent, les boîtes Statistics and Machine Learning et Econometrics ; le script main.m emploie aussi Curve Fitting. run_benchmark reconstruit le tableau hors échantillon ; main est une démonstration dans l’échantillon.
% Dépôt cyclostationary-forecasting-matlab, version 1.1.1
run_benchmark
% Sur votre série x, période T, horizon h et longueur d'apprentissage n_train :
[pred, lambda] = predict_P_BLEND_LS(x, T, h, n_train);
Résultats du code ouvert v1.1.1
Expérience distincte de l’article. Les poids sont estimés sur les 250 premiers cycles et évalués sur les 250 suivants, pour dix réalisations d’un générateur synthétique « ciel clair × bruit corrélé ». BLEND avec un poids par phase bat la persistance cyclique à tous les horizons testés. CLIPER sur le rapport à la tendance de ciel clair obtient ici les plus faibles erreurs moyennes ; ce résultat est cohérent avec le générateur choisi et ne constitue pas un classement universel.
Références hors échantillon, signal synthétique de jour et de nuit, moyenne ± écart type sur dix réalisations. Figure en PDF.
nRMSE moyenne selon l’horizon (pas de temps, \(T=24\)), jour et nuit. x est la série, CS sa référence de ciel clair ; « Ciel clair » indique que l’opérateur l’utilise.
Différence à la tendance : la tendance est représentée ici par le profil moyen du cycle, estimé heure par heure. On le soustrait à la valeur observée, soit \(x(t)-\mu(\text{phase})\). Ce profil est estimé uniquement sur les données d’entraînement. Pour prévoir, CLIPER ajoute au profil moyen de l’heure cible une fraction de l’écart observé à l’instant présent. Cet écart peut être positif ou négatif ; il ne désigne pas une erreur de mesure.

La version 1.1.1 (archive de la version) corrige des erreurs des versions 1.0.0 et 1.1.0 : usage de valeurs déjà connues, poids BLEND placé sur le mauvais terme, corrélations indéfinies ramenées à 1 et estimation CLIPER cyclostationnaire. Le dépôt documente deux écarts avec l’article imprimé, à l’équation (2) et à la définition 5. Le tableau ci-dessus est un contrôle du code corrigé sur un générateur synthétique précis ; il ne remplace pas la validation des 68 stations. Données et scripts complets.
Sur une série photovoltaïque réelle : quand BLEND gagne-t-il ?
Avec la référence de ciel clair, CLIPER sur le rapport à la tendance x/CS bat BLEND sur x/CS de 1 à 2 % à tous les horizons, sur l’ensemble des journées de test réunies. BLEND gagne seulement dans la classe des journées stables, connue après observation. Sans ciel clair, BLEND ajusté avec un poids par phase bat CLIPER sur la différence à la tendance à partir de 3 h ; il perd à 1 et 2 h.
Dans ce test, l’intérêt de BLEND ajusté est donc conditionnel : sans référence de ciel clair et à partir de 3 h, son gain atteint 1,5 % à 3 h, 8,1 % à 6 h et 10,0 % à 9 h. Il faut estimer T poids, un par phase (24 ici), contre un pour CLIPER. Par classe, il gagne sur les journées stables à partir de 2 h, sur les intermédiaires à partir de 6 h, et jamais sur les journées variables.
La forme simplifiée ne partage pas ces gains. Avec λ = (1 + ρ)/2 (définition 8), BLEND bat la persistance simple aux cinq horizons, mais ne bat pas la persistance cyclique de 2 à 9 h sur l’ensemble du test : nRMSE de 0,709 à 2 h et 1,041 à 6 h, contre 0,690. L’article présente des séries synthétiques et 68 stations d’éclairement SIAR ; ce test porte sur d’autres données, un seul site PV, et ne démontre pas la cause des différences.
BLEND est une combinaison convexe de la persistance (la dernière valeur) et de la persistance cyclique (la veille à la même heure) ; CLIPER, de la persistance et de la moyenne : sa variante centrée ajoute au profil moyen cible une fraction de la différence actuelle à ce profil. Données : exemple public de Palaiseau de PV_ELM_pred, puissance AC moyennée à l’heure, UTC, août 2020 à septembre 2025, T = 24. Les opérateurs v1.1.1 sont ajustés sur la première moitié (environ 2,6 ans), puis évalués sur la seconde. Les journées de test sont classées selon la variabilité de leur propre rapport à la tendance de ciel clair (écart-type des variations horaires), avec des seuils de terciles fixés sur l’apprentissage : 329 journées stables, 372 intermédiaires et 238 variables. Les tableaux concernent les heures de jour.

Mémoire et prévisibilité par type de journée
Comment lire ces nombres.
k, rapport à la tendance (indice de ciel clair)
k = P / Pcs : puissance rapportée à la référence de ciel clair. Le rapport retire une grande partie du cycle solaire ; sa valeur dépend aussi de la qualité de cette référence. Il est indéfini lorsque le dénominateur est nul.
ρ1 et ρ24, mémoire
Corrélation de Pearson (de −1 à 1) de k avec sa valeur une heure ou 24 heures auparavant, sur les paires diurnes. Une corrélation de 1 correspond à une relation linéaire positive parfaite, pas forcément à des valeurs identiques ; 0 signifie absence de corrélation linéaire, sans exclure une dépendance non linéaire. ρ24 renseigne sur la ressemblance entre journées.
sCV, variabilité
sCV = √2 / |d − 1| × RMSE(P − Pcs) / RMS(Pcs), avec d = 0,2 : différence à la tendance de ciel clair, normalisée. La référence d’alternance aléatoire entre ciel clair et couvert vaut 1 ; ce n’est pas un maximum universel. Un couvert stable et des passages nuageux peuvent avoir le même sCV.
F, prévisibilité
F = 1 + sCV × (ρmax − 1), où ρmax est le maximum de l’autocorrélation absolue du résidu P − Pcs entre les retards h et 12 h. F est compris entre 1 − sCV et 1. Il renseigne sur la prévisibilité, sans garantir la performance d’un modèle. Pour h ≥ 3 dans ces données, le maximum est atteint au retard 12 h dans chaque classe : F est donc identique à 3, 6 et 9 h.
nRMSE
Racine de l’erreur quadratique moyenne divisée par la puissance moyenne observée sur les mêmes heures. Une nRMSE de 0,30 signifie que la RMSE représente 30 % de cette moyenne.
sCV et F proviennent de Voyant et ses coauteurs, Renewable Energy (2026), doi:10.1016/j.renene.2025.123913 · BibTeX. Voir les définitions et le calculateur dans sCV et F : variabilité et prévisibilité, ainsi que le code de référence.
Moitié de test, heures de jour : ρ24 et ρ1 mesurent la mémoire du rapport à la tendance de ciel clair à 24 h et 1 h ; F dépend de l’horizon h ; sCV décrit la variabilité.
Type de journée | ρ24 | ρ1 | F (h = 1) | F (h ≥ 3) | sCV | heures |
Journées stables | 0,38 | 0,95 | 0,88 | 0,67 | 1,17 | 4068 |
Journées intermédiaires | 0,36 | 0,83 | 0,85 | 0,60 | 1,11 | 5089 |
Journées variables | 0,10 | 0,67 | 0,80 | 0,32 | 1,11 | 2705 |
Toutes les journées | 0,28 | 0,83 | 0,85 | 0,58 | 1,13 | 11862 |
sCV varie peu entre classes (environ 1,1), mais ρ24 passe de 0,38 sur les journées stables à 0,10 sur les variables, et F de 0,67 à 0,32 à trois heures et au-delà. C’est une description de trois classes, pas une démonstration causale. ρ24 ne sépare pas à lui seul les gagnants : il est proche pour les journées stables et intermédiaires (0,38 et 0,36), alors que BLEND sur x/CS gagne uniquement sur les stables. Définitions de sCV et F.
Ce que ce test ne démontre pas.
Les classes utilisent la variabilité de la journée observée : diagnostic a posteriori, pas méthode de choix en avance. Ce choix demanderait une prévision du type de journée.
Le ciel clair est un proxy : éclairement global horizontal (GHI) du modèle pvlib Ineichen, mise à l’échelle par le 99e percentile de P/GHIcs sur l’apprentissage. L’orientation des panneaux n’est pas modélisée.
Un site, des données horaires, une seule coupure apprentissage/test, des poids ajustés une fois sur tous les jours d’apprentissage et aucun test de significativité : les plus faibles écarts peuvent ne pas se retrouver ailleurs. La charge, le vent et la température ne sont pas testés ici.
Données et scripts : nRMSE de 11 références par horizon et classe (CSV) · ρ, F et sCV (CSV) · prep.py · run_real.m · run_forecastability.m. Opérateurs v1.1.1 ; code sCV et F.
Une échelle de références
Comparer des références de sophistication croissante et toutes les rapporter. Les cinq premières viennent de « Benchmarks for solar radiation time series forecasting » (Voyant, Notton, Duchaud, Garcia-Gutierrez, Bright et Yang, Renewable Energy 191, 747–762, 2022, DOI · BibTeX) et d’ARTU ; BLEND est introduit dans l’article de 2026.
Référence | Principe | Estimé sur les données |
Persistance (PER) | prolonger le dernier rapport à la tendance (indice de ciel clair) | aucun paramètre |
Climatologie (CLIM) | moyenne du rapport à la tendance sur l’apprentissage | une moyenne |
CLIPER | combinaison convexe de la persistance et de la moyenne (climatologie), pondérée par l’autocorrélation au retard h | une corrélation |
Lissage exponentiel (ES) | valeurs récentes pondérées exponentiellement | une corrélation |
ARTU | extension d’ordre deux utilisant les autocorrélations aux retards h et 2h ; coefficients lus dans une table | deux corrélations |
BLEND (cyclostationnaire) | combinaison convexe de la persistance et de la persistance cyclique ; poids analytique ½(1 + ρ) par phase, ou poids optimal en MSE de l’équation (2) | statistiques cycliques ou ajustement analytique aux moindres carrés |
Quand l’utiliser, et ses limites
Les moyennes, variances et corrélations cycliques exigent suffisamment de cycles passés pour être estimées. Un modèle autorégressif ou à apprentissage peut faire mieux dans d’autres conditions. Sur vos données, fixer les mêmes horizons, fenêtres, masques de valeurs manquantes et références avant de conclure. BLEND fournit une référence analytique reproductible, pas une promesse de supériorité universelle.
Article, équipe et code
Cyril Voyant, Candice Banes, Luis Garcia-Gutierrez, Gilles Notton, Milan Despotovic et Zaher Mundher Yaseen, « Symmetry-constrained forecasting of periodically correlated energy processes », Applied Mathematical Modelling 157, 116988 (2026), doi:10.1016/j.apm.2026.116988 · BibTeX. Prépublication. La contribution est collective.

Title: BLEND and CLIPER: cyclostationary persistence references for solar forecasting
Language: en

Description: Persistence is the reference every solar forecast must beat. BLEND, a cyclostationary persistence operator with weights estimated from historical data…

Solar forecasting explained · Published article, open code (v1.1.1)
BLEND and CLIPER: cyclostationary persistence references for solar forecasting
BLEND was introduced by Voyant et al. in Applied Mathematical Modelling (2026).
Principle 3 · Complexity only if it paysThe approachIn the story: climb only if it pays. A persistence reference built on the cyclostationary structure of the signal is the first level any trained model must beat.
In brief
BLEND extends persistence to cyclostationary series: the forecast is a convex combination of simple persistence I(t) and cyclic persistence I(t−T+nΔt), with the closed-form weight λ̃ = ½(1 + ρ(t, nΔt)) of the latest value, ρ being the local correlation at that phase.
It preserves the periodic variance and covariance, needs no training and no clear-sky model, and on 68 SIAR stations gives accuracy gains over classical persistence, particularly at multi-hour horizons.
Published in Applied Mathematical Modelling 157, 116988 (2026) by C. Voyant, C. Banes, L. Garcia-Gutierrez, G. Notton, M. Despotovic and Z. M. Yaseen; audited MATLAB code v1.1.1, doi:10.5281/zenodo.18812333.
Why compare a solar forecast with persistence? BLEND and cyclostationary persistence
What does BLEND add?
The study develops analytical reference forecasts that exploit periodic statistics. The article derives the MSE-optimal weight between simple and cyclic persistence for stationary and periodically stationary processes, and its analytical limit, the closed-form coefficient λ̃ = ½(1 + ρ(t, τ)), where ρ is the local correlation between the current observation and its phase-aligned lag: a training-free baseline that preserves the periodic variance and covariance.
Figure 6 of the author version (Voyant et al., Applied Mathematical Modelling, 2026): average nRMSE and nMAE over the 68 SIAR stations, horizons 30 to 360 min, BLEND variants and reference models.
Follow the numerical example
Cyril Voyant · Published 2026-10-19
BLEND, the cyclostationary persistence operator of Cyril Voyant and co-authors (Applied Mathematical Modelling, 2026, doi:10.1016/j.apm.2026.116988 · BibTeX), is a convex combination of ordinary persistence and cyclic persistence (same phase, previous cycle), giving a reference forecast with weights estimated from historical data for periodically correlated energy series.
Questions about persistence in solar forecasting
Why compare a solar forecast with persistence?
Persistence costs nothing and is hard to beat at short horizons. A forecast that does not beat a well-defined persistence reference, on the same samples and horizons, adds no demonstrated skill. Report the gain against that reference, for example with the NICEᵏ metrics, and state which persistence you used: simple, clear-sky (“smart”) or cyclostationary.
What is cyclostationary persistence?
Solar irradiance, wind and load do not keep the same statistics through the day: mean, variance and correlation repeat with the cycle. Cyclostationary persistence uses that structure. BLEND weights the latest observation and the same-phase observation of the previous cycle; in its simplest closed form the weight of the latest value is λ̃ = ½(1 + ρ), with ρ the local correlation at that phase (Definition 8 of the article). No network is trained.
The theory
Why, in the words of the article: solar irradiance, wind speed and electrical load have strong diurnal and seasonal periodicities, and their statistics vary with the phase of the cycle, which stationary models and classical persistence cannot capture. The article extends persistence to these cyclostationary processes with closed-form operators that preserve the periodic variance and covariance: a symmetry-induced reduction of the degrees of freedom, and a training-free analytical limit of persistence. Definition and equation numbers are those of the article (arXiv:2602.18949).
Cyclostationarity (Theorem 1)
A process \(I(t)\) of period \(T\) is periodically stationary when its first and second moments repeat with the cycle: \(\mu(t)=\mu(t+T)\), \(\sigma^2(t)=\sigma^2(t+T)\), \(C(t,n\Delta t)=C(t+T,n\Delta t)\), with the phase-dependent correlation
$$\rho(t,n\Delta t)=\frac{C(t,n\Delta t)}{\sigma(t)\,\sigma(t+n\Delta t)} .$$
Here \(I(t)\) is the series, \(\Delta t\) its time step, \(n\) the horizon in steps, \(T\) the period, and \(\mu,\sigma^2,C\) the mean, variance and covariance at each phase. Time is read on the cyclic group \(\mathbb Z/T\mathbb Z\): \(t\) and \(t-T\) are the same phase.
The persistence operators (Definitions 1 to 5)
Simple persistence P (Def. 1): \(\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=I(t)\).
Cyclic persistence P⟲ (Def. 2): \(\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=I(t-T+n\Delta t)\), the same phase one cycle earlier.
Smart persistence (Def. 3): \(\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=\dfrac{I(t)}{I_{\mathrm{ref}}(t)}\,I_{\mathrm{ref}}(t+n\Delta t)\), with a reference such as clear sky.
CLIPER, stationary (Def. 4): \(\lambda\,\mu+(1-\lambda)I(t)\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{CLIPER}}=1-\rho(n\Delta t)\); cyclostationary (Def. 5): \(\lambda^{\circlearrowleft}\mu(t)+(1-\lambda^{\circlearrowleft})I(t)\), with $$\lambda^{\circlearrowleft}_{\mathrm{CLIPER}}=\dfrac{[\mu(t+n\Delta t)-\mu(t)]^2+\sigma^2(t)-\rho(t,n\Delta t)\,\sigma(t)\sigma(t+n\Delta t)}{[\mu(t+n\Delta t)-\mu(t)]^2+\sigma^2(t)}$$
.
BLEND (Definitions 6 to 8)
BLEND is a convex combination of cyclic and simple persistence; \(\lambda\) weights simple persistence:
$$\hat I(t+n\Delta t)=\big(1-\lambda\big)\,I(t-T+n\Delta t)+\lambda\,I(t).$$
Stationary BLEND (Def. 6), MSE-optimal weight from the autocorrelation:
$$\lambda_{\mathrm{BLEND}}=\frac{\rho(T)-\rho(n\Delta t)+\rho(n\Delta t-T)-1}{2\big(\rho(n\Delta t-T)-1\big)} .$$
Periodically stationary BLEND (Def. 7, Eqs. 1 and 2): the weight varies with the phase and carries the periodic means, variances and correlations,
with \(D=(\mu(t)-\mu(t+n\Delta t))^2+\sigma^2(t)+\sigma^2(t+n\Delta t)\), the weight of Eq. (2) reads
$$\lambda^{\circlearrowleft}_{\mathrm{BLEND}}=\frac{(\mu(t)-\mu(t+n\Delta t))^2+\sigma^2(t+n\Delta t)\,[1-\rho(t+n\Delta t,T)]}{D}+\frac{\sigma(t)\sigma(t+n\Delta t)\,[\rho(t,n\Delta t)-\rho(t,n\Delta t-T)]}{D+2\rho(t,n\Delta t-T)\,\sigma(t)\sigma(t+n\Delta t)},$$
$$(2)$$
Simplified BLEND (Def. 8), the analytical limit and the central result of the article:
$$\tilde\lambda^{\circlearrowleft}_{\mathrm{BLEND}}=\tfrac12\big(1+\rho(t,n\Delta t)\big),$$
an optimal shrinkage between instantaneous memory and phase-aligned recurrence (Remark 18): high correlation favors short-term persistence, low or negative correlation the periodic component. It holds under three conditions (Remark 17): equal means and variances at \(t\) and \(t+n\Delta t\); correlation symmetry \(\rho(t+n\Delta t,T)=\rho(t,n\Delta t-T)\); negligible long-lag correlation, \(\rho(t,n\Delta t-T)\approx0\) for \(1\ll n\Delta t\ll T\).
Properties (Appendix D)
With \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) the operator is stable: each forecast lies between \(I(t)\) and \(I(t-T)\) (Theorem 11). It returns a constant signal unchanged. When the denominator of Eq. (2) approaches zero (weak periodic contrast), a mild clipping of \(\lambda\) to \([0,1]\) keeps it stable (Remark 16).
What the article shows
Validation on synthetic cyclostationary series (hybrid bootstrap and Monte Carlo) and on 30-minute irradiation from 68 SIAR stations in Spain (2017–2020), horizons from 30 minutes to 6 hours: embedding the cyclic variance and covariance gives measurable accuracy gains over classical persistence, particularly at multi-hour horizons, even without clear-sky normalization. On the synthetic series, the periodically stationary BLEND and its simplified form are the best models at 1 h and 3 h (Kruskal-Wallis, then pairwise Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon tests); on the measured data, the simplified BLEND offers the most practical balance, accurate across horizons without clear-sky input and at minimal cost (Wilcoxon tests, p < 0.01). AR(p), extreme learning machines or smart persistence can do better under optimized conditions, but they need fitting, prior normalization or learned representations; BLEND reaches comparable robustness at negligible cost, as a reproducible analytical baseline.
Try it in your browser
Keep the demo data, paste a periodic series or load 40 days of real photovoltaic data (Palaiseau, public example of PV_ELM_pred); see three whole days of forecasts, set λ yourself on the error parabola of one phase against the least-squares weight, and read the gain of BLEND over the better persistence at every horizon.
Run it
Requires MATLAB R2021a or later with the Statistics and Machine Learning, Econometrics and (for main.m only) Curve Fitting toolboxes. run_benchmark rebuilds the out-of-sample table of the next section; main is the in-sample demonstration.
% from a clone of github.com/cyrilvoyant/cyclostationary-forecasting-matlab (v1.1.1)
run_benchmark % out-of-sample, 10 seeds -> results/benchmark_v111_summary.csv (the table below)
% one operator on your own series x (column vector), period T, horizon h, first n_train values for fitting
[pred, lambda] = predict_P_BLEND_LS(x, T, h, n_train);
Key finding
Accounting for the daily phase improves persistence forecasts on the solar series studied, and the differences widen at longer horizons. In the Applied Mathematical Modelling paper, validation combines controlled cyclostationary simulations with measurements from 68 Spanish stations; on measured data, cyclostationary adjustments reduce errors relative to their naive counterparts, and inter-model differences are tested with Wilcoxon tests. BLEND works directly on raw irradiance, without normalizing by an external clear-sky model.
Results of the open code (v1.1.1, audited)
All BLEND operators share the forecast of the article, Î(t+h) = (1 − λ)·I(t+h−T) + λ·I(t): λ multiplies the latest value. CLIPER is a convex combination of persistence (the latest value) and the mean. The weight is one value for the whole series or one value per phase, and it is estimated on past data. In an out-of-sample benchmark (weights estimated on the first 250 cycles, scored on the next 250, 10 realizations), BLEND with a weight per phase improves on cyclic persistence at every horizon. CLIPER applied to the ratio to trend x/CS (clear-sky reference) has the lowest mean errors, which is consistent with a signal generated as clear sky × correlated noise; stationary BLEND applied to x/CS is much better than BLEND on the raw signal. The simplified weight (1 + ρ)/2 is exact under the assumptions of Remark 17 of the article. These are results of the corrected open code on one synthetic generator (clear sky × correlated noise), different from the article's generators and from its 68 measured stations; they do not replace the article's validation, where the simplified BLEND is among the best at 1 h and 3 h and offers the most practical balance on measured data.
Out-of-sample benchmark of the persistence references, synthetic signal, day and night, mean ± standard deviation over 10 realizations (PDF).
Difference to trend: here, the trend is represented by the mean cycle profile, estimated hour by hour. Subtract this profile from the observed value, giving \(x(t)-\mu(\text{phase})\). This profile is estimated only from the training data. To forecast, CLIPER adds a fraction of the current departure to the mean profile at the target hour. The departure can be positive or negative; it does not mean a measurement error.

Version 1.1.1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23534072; all versions) corrects errors of v1.0.0 and v1.1.0: forecasts compared with already known values, the BLEND weight placed on the wrong term, undefined correlations clipped to 1, and estimation errors in the cyclostationary CLIPER. The code was audited independently and every number above was reproduced. It also documents two differences with the printed article (Eq. 2 and Definition 5). These are results on one synthetic generator, not a validation on measured data nor a universal ranking. Data: all 21 references, day and night and daytime only (CSV) · README and table on GitHub · step-by-step example.
Who wins when: a real photovoltaic series
With a clear-sky reference, CLIPER on x/CS beats BLEND on x/CS at all horizons across all test days combined, by 1 to 2 %, and it is simpler. BLEND wins only on stable days, a class known only after the fact. Without clear sky, BLEND with one weight per phase beats CLIPER on the difference to trend from h = 3 and loses at h = 1 and 2.
BLEND therefore stays useful under conditions, on this test: no clear-sky reference and a horizon of at least 3 h. Its gain then grows with the horizon (1.5 % at h = 3, 8.1 % at h = 6, 10.0 % at h = 9). It costs T weights, one per phase (24 here), against one for CLIPER. By day type, this BLEND wins on stable days from h = 2, on intermediate days from h = 6, and never on variable days.
The simplified form does not share these gains. With λ = (1 + ρ)/2 (Definition 8), BLEND beats simple persistence at all horizons, but it does not beat cyclic persistence at h = 2 to 9 in this test, on all test days (0.709 at h = 2 and 1.041 at h = 6, against 0.690). The article reports its results on synthetic series and on 68 irradiance stations (SIAR); this test uses other data, one PV site, and does not establish why the results differ.
BLEND is a convex combination of persistence (the latest value) and cyclic persistence (yesterday at the same hour); CLIPER is a convex combination of persistence and the mean.
Test: the public Palaiseau PV example of PV_ELM_pred (AC power, hourly means, UTC, August 2020 to September 2025, T = 24). The audited v1.1.1 operators, unchanged, are fitted on the first half (2.6 years) and scored on the second, as in the synthetic benchmark above. Test days are sorted by the variability of their own ratio to trend (clear-sky index) (standard deviation of its hour-to-hour changes), in terciles fixed on the training days: 329 stable, 372 intermediate and 238 variable days. Daytime hours only.

Memory and forecastability by day type
How to read these numbers.
k, ratio to trend (clear-sky index)
k = P / Pcs: the share of the clear-sky power actually produced. 1 under a clear sky, around 0.2 under a thick cloud. Removing the clear sky removes most of the daily and yearly cycle, so what remains is the weather.
ρ1 and ρ24, memory
Correlation (Pearson, from −1 to 1) between k and its own value 1 hour earlier (ρ1) or 24 hours earlier, at the same time of day (ρ24), over daytime pairs. 1: a perfect positive linear relationship, not necessarily identical values; 0: no linear correlation at that lag; nonlinear dependence may still exist. ρ1 is the memory used by persistence; ρ24 asks “does today look like yesterday at the same hour?”, the memory used by the cyclic term of BLEND.
sCV, variability
sCV = √2 / |d − 1| · RMSE(P − Pcs) / RMS(Pcs), with d = 0.2: how far the series stays from clear sky, whatever the cause. 0 when the sky is always clear; 1 for a sky switching at random between clear and thick cloud (the reference of strong variability, not a maximum). A steady overcast day and a broken-cloud day can have the same sCV.
F, forecastability
F = 1 + sCV · (ρmax − 1), where ρmax is the largest |autocorrelation| of the residual P − Pcs between lag h and 12 h. F lies between 1 − sCV (variable and without memory: hard) and 1 (no variability or perfect memory: easy). Higher F indicates greater forecastability under this diagnostic; it does not guarantee the performance of a particular model. For h ≥ 3, ρmax is reached at the 12-hour lag in every class, so F is the same for h = 3, 6 and 9.
nRMSE
Root mean square error divided by the mean observed power on the same hours: 0.30 means a typical error of 30 % of the mean production.
sCV and F come from Voyant et al., Renewable Energy (2026), doi:10.1016/j.renene.2025.123913 · BibTeX; explained, with an interactive calculator, on the page sCV and F: variability and forecastability of solar irradiance (in French: variabilité et prévisibilité). Reference code: solar-variability-scv.
Test half, daytime. ρ24 and ρ1: memory of the ratio to trend over 24 h and 1 h. F: forecastability at horizon h. sCV: variability. Definitions above.
Day type | ρ24 | ρ1 | F (h = 1) | F (h ≥ 3) | sCV | hours |
Stable days | 0.38 | 0.95 | 0.88 | 0.67 | 1.17 | 4068 |
Intermediate days | 0.36 | 0.83 | 0.85 | 0.60 | 1.11 | 5089 |
Variable days | 0.10 | 0.67 | 0.80 | 0.32 | 1.11 | 2705 |
All days | 0.28 | 0.83 | 0.85 | 0.58 | 1.13 | 11862 |
sCV hardly changes between classes (about 1.1). The memory does change: ρ24 falls from 0.38 on stable days to 0.10 on variable days, and F at three hours and beyond from 0.67 to 0.32. This is a description of three classes, not a cause. ρ24 alone does not separate the winners: it is close on stable and intermediate days (0.38 and 0.36), yet BLEND on x/CS wins only on stable days. Definitions and the reference code: sCV and forecastability F.
What this test does not show.
The classes use the variability of the day itself: a diagnosis after the fact, not a forecasting method. Choosing the reference in advance would need a forecast of the day type.
The clear-sky reference is a proxy: pvlib Ineichen clear-sky GHI at the site, scaled to power by the 99th percentile of P/GHIcs on the training half; the panel orientation is not modelled.
One site, hourly data, one train/test split, weights fitted once on all training days, and no significance test: the smallest differences may not hold elsewhere. Load, wind and temperature are not tested here.
Data and scripts: nRMSE of 11 references by horizon and day type (CSV) · ρ, F and sCV (CSV) · prep.py · run_real.m · run_forecastability.m (operators: v1.1.1; sCV and F: solar-variability-scv).
A ladder of reference forecasts
Use references in increasing order of sophistication, and report each one. The first five are documented in Benchmarks for solar radiation time series forecasting (Cyril Voyant, Gilles Notton, Jean-Laurent Duchaud, Luis Antonio Garcia-Gutierrez, Jamie M. Bright, Dazhi Yang, Renewable Energy 191, 747–762, 2022, doi:10.1016/j.renene.2022.04.065 · BibTeX) and implemented in ARTU; BLEND comes from the 2026 paper.
Reference | Idea | Estimated from data |
Persistence (PER) | carry the last ratio to trend (clear-sky index) forward | nothing |
Climatology (CLIM) | mean ratio to trend of the training sample | one mean |
CLIPER | convex combination of persistence and the mean (climatology), weighted by the lag-h autocorrelation | one correlation |
Exponential smoothing (ES) | exponentially weighted recent values | one correlation |
ARTU | second-order extension using lag-h and lag-2h autocorrelations, coefficients read from a lookup table | two correlations |
BLEND (cyclostationary) | convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence, with the closed-form weight ½(1 + ρ) per phase, or the MSE-optimal weight of Eq. (2) | cyclic statistics or a closed-form least-squares fit |
Limits
“Training-free” does not mean “observation-free”: cyclic means, deviations and correlations must still be estimated on past data, and they need enough cycles to be stable. BLEND does not outperform every optimized method; autoregressive or learned predictors can do better under some conditions. The evidence concerns the datasets of the paper, not a universal ranking of forecasting methods. Test the transfer to your own series rather than assuming it.

Title: Dimensionality reduction for direct PV power forecasting
Language: en
Other language: fr: https://www.cyrilvoyant.com/prevision-pv-reduction-dimension/
Description: Why forecast delivered PV power directly, and compress its history? Redundancy, geometric filters, forecast validation and a worked numerical example.

Solar forecasting explained · 20 October 2026 · Full English version
Dimensionality reduction for direct PV power forecasting
Principle 4 · Every tool, at the peripheryThe approachIn the story: learn frugally, the input is compressed only when the compression serves the forecast.
In brief
A direct PV forecast reads the plant's own recent history; dimensionality reduction compresses that lagged history before a forecaster reads it.
Seven reductions (principal component analysis PCA, kernel PCA, Isomap, locally linear embedding LLE, Laplacian eigenmaps, diffusion maps, autoencoder) are judged twice: does the reduced space keep the geometry, and does it help the forecast?
H. Bouzgou, G. Chesnoiu, C. F. Nicolosi, A. Chatel, G. Notton, L. Menard and C. Voyant, manuscript in preparation; MATLAB code, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21755938.
Direct PV power forecasting: why reduce dimensionality?
A day of measurements contains many values, but not necessarily as many independent pieces of information. Dimensionality reduction seeks a compact representation, then checks whether it remains useful for forecasting.
Why forecast PV power directly?
Battery scheduling and grid injection decisions often need the electrical power actually delivered by a plant. One route forecasts solar irradiance, transposes it to the module plane, then models electrical conversion. Another forecasts future power directly from the plant’s past production.
Measured productionUseful historyFuture power
The direct route avoids reconstructing the entire conversion chain for this task. The measurements already reflect the recent response of the modules and inverter. This does not make weather information irrelevant: sky observations, satellites and numerical weather predictions can provide information that the plant’s own history does not contain.
Delivered power is not the available solar resource. A production drop may reflect a cloud, curtailment, a fault or maintenance. These causes cannot always be distinguished from power measurements alone.
Why compress the history?
Imagine feeding a model every half-hourly measurement from the previous day. Neighboring values often move together. Treating each as a completely separate input may increase the input size without adding proportionate information. Dimensionality reduction constructs a smaller set of coordinates representing that trajectory.
Several nearly identical photographs do not necessarily provide several new views of an object. Yet removing one may also discard an important detail. Compression must be evaluated, rather than assumed beneficial.
Two questions, two diagnostics
Is the geometry preserved? A model-free filter assesses local neighborhoods and global distances.
Is the representation useful for forecasting? A wrapper evaluates it with a forecasting model, here an Extreme Learning Machine (ELM).
Geometric fidelity does not automatically imply predictive usefulness. The repository compares PCA, manifold methods and an autoencoder using these complementary perspectives.
The theory
The input of a direct PV forecast is the lagged history \(\mathbf x_t=[y_{t},y_{t-1},\dots,y_{t-D+1}]\in\mathbb R^{D}\) (for a day at 30 minutes, \(D=48\)). A reduction maps it to \(\mathbf z_t=\Phi(\mathbf x_t)\in\mathbb R^{d}\), \(d\ll D\), then a forecaster reads \(\mathbf z_t\).
Seven reductions
PCA (linear: \(\mathbf z=U_d^{\top}(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})\), with \(U_d\) the first \(d\) principal directions), Kernel PCA, Isomap, LLE, Laplacian Eigenmaps, Diffusion Maps and an autoencoder. Nonlinear embeddings are computed on a subsample and extended to every point (out-of-sample operator or k-NN interpolation).
Filter: is the geometry preserved?
$$S(d)=\alpha\,T(k)+(1-\alpha)\,\rho,$$
with \(\alpha\) the weight between the two terms, \(T(k)\) the trustworthiness of the \(k\)-nearest neighbourhoods (are the neighbours in \(\mathbf z\) true neighbours in \(\mathbf x\)?) and \(\rho\) a Mantel-type correlation between the distance matrices of \(\mathbf x\) and \(\mathbf z\). Because \(S(d)\) grows mechanically with \(d\), the rule keeps the smallest \(d\) that reaches a fraction \(q\) of the achievable score.
Wrapper: is it useful for forecasting?
For each \(d\), an ELM (and a linear AR) is trained on \(\mathbf z_t\) plus the time features, and \(d\) is chosen to minimise \(\mathrm{NICE}^{\Sigma}\) (NICE guide). A good geometry does not imply a good forecast: the two diagnostics are kept apart and reported against the parameter count.
Assumptions and validity
The reduction is fitted on training data only; the dimension is selected on the evaluation set that is reported, a choice the repository states. The manuscript is in preparation: this page gives the method, not its results.
Worked example: from 48 inputs to 4 coordinates
A day sampled every 30 minutes gives 48 power values. Reducing them to 4 coordinates means 12 times fewer inputs. This is a dimensionality ratio, not a measured speedup.
For a 100-neuron hidden layer, the input weights number 4,800 before reduction and 400 afterward, excluding biases, output weights and any calendar inputs. But a linear 48-to-4 projection itself stores 192 coefficients, potentially plus centering and scaling information. A nonlinear transformation may cost more.
Suppose test RMSE is 100 W without reduction and 102 W with reduction: error rises by 2% in exchange for a more compact representation. Whether that is acceptable depends on the application. These are illustrative values, not manuscript results.
What makes the comparison credible?
Fit the transformation only on past training data. Reserve future dates for testing and use identical horizons and evaluation samples. Include the unreduced model and simple baselines. Count the transformation’s cost: a smaller input does not guarantee a cheaper complete pipeline.
The choice depends on site, horizon and data quality. Compression does not solve missing history at a new plant or undocumented changes in plant operation.
Explore the collaborative work
The MATLAB repository includes a Palaiseau example and a quick smoke-test mode. Its seven-method comparison separates geometric preservation from forecasting utility. The associated manuscript is in preparation; this page reports no unpublished numerical findings.
The project code uses the MIT license. The bundled drtoolbox retains its own non-commercial terms; check them before reuse.
MATLAB code and protocolNext: why deploy frugal models?

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/methods/pv-elm.html
Title: PV_ELM_pred: benchmarking persistence, autoregression and ELM for PV forecasting
Language: en
Description: Open Python benchmark of persistence, linear AR and 14 Extreme Learning Machine variants for frugal PV, irradiance and weather forecasting at the edge.

Solar forecasting explained · Open benchmark code, manuscript in preparation
PV_ELM_pred: benchmarking persistence, autoregression and ELM for PV forecasting
Principle 4 · Every tool, at the peripheryThe approachIn the story: when no equation links the data, learn it frugally, every model's parameters are counted next to its error.
In brief
PV_ELM_pred puts persistence, BLEND, a linear autoregression and 14 extreme learning machine variants through the same chronological splits, inputs and metrics.
A capacity sweep from 5 to 1,000 hidden neurons plots the error relative to simple persistence (NICE^Σ) against the number of stored parameters, to measure how much model a forecast really needs.
M. Leiva, X. Silvani, G. Notton, C. Voyant and A. Julien, software v1.0.0, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21487267; the associated manuscript is in preparation and no result of it is reported here.
How much model is enough for solar forecasting? The PV_ELM_pred benchmark
What does the software contribute?
PV_ELM_pred provides a common protocol to compare persistence, BLEND, autoregression and ELM variants. It is software; the associated frugality manuscript is in preparation. A larger parameter count alone is not an energy measurement.
Figure of the PV_ELM_pred repository (figures/Palaiseau, labels in French): measured AC power on a variable day at Palaiseau and the ELM forecast one hour ahead. The forecast follows the ramps one step late; it does not anticipate them.
Cyril Voyant · Updated 2026-10-20
PV_ELM_pred (M. Leiva, X. Silvani, G. Notton, C. Voyant, A. Julien, 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21487267) benchmarks persistence, BLEND, linear autoregression and 14 Extreme Learning Machine variants on the same splits and metrics, so that every gain in skill can be weighed against the extra model it costs.
Questions and answers
How should ELM and linear autoregression be benchmarked for PV forecasting?
On the same chronological splits, inputs and metrics, with persistence and a cyclostationary persistence such as BLEND as references. Fit scaling on the training fold only, use several random seeds for the ELM, and report daytime-only and all-hours scores separately. PV_ELM_pred implements this protocol for AR-OLS and 14 ELM variants.
How can forecasting skill be compared with model complexity in energy forecasting?
Plot a persistence-normalized skill score (for example NICE^Σ from the NICEᵏ family) against the logarithm of the stored parameter count, across a sweep of model sizes and seeds, with persistence and linear AR as fixed references. PV_ELM_pred runs such a sweep from 5 to 1000 hidden neurons. A parameter count is not an energy measurement: report latency and memory separately.
What this benchmark answers
How much model is enough to forecast a measured solar or weather channel from its own past, from 30 minutes to several hours ahead? PV_ELM_pred puts persistence, a linear autoregression and 14 Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) variants through the same pipeline, the same splits and the same metrics, so that every gain in skill can be weighed against the extra model it costs.
It is a frugal-AI testbed for edge forecasting: the models run on a CPU, use only the target's own history and cyclic time features, and need no numerical weather prediction.
The theory
Reference forecasts
At origin \(t\) and horizon \(h\), with cycle length \(T\) (24 hourly steps for a day):
$$\hat y^{\,\mathrm{P}}_{t+h}=y_t\quad(\text{persistence}),$$
$$\hat y^{\,\mathrm{C}}_{t+h}=y_{t+h-T}\quad(\text{cyclic persistence: same phase, previous cycle}).$$
Linear autoregression (AR-OLS)
$$\hat y_{t+h}=a_0+\sum_{i=1}^{p}a_i\,y_{t-i+1}+\mathbf c^{\top}\mathbf p_{t+h},$$
$$\mathbf a=X^{+}\mathbf y,$$
with \(p\) the number of lags, \(a_0,a_i,\mathbf c\) the fitted coefficients, \(\mathbf p_{t+h}\) the cyclic time features of the target time and \(X^{+}\) the pseudo-inverse of the design matrix.
Extreme learning machine (ELM)
For an input row \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^{d}\), a hidden layer of \(L\) neurons with weights \(W\in\mathbb R^{L\times d}\) and biases \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^{L}\) drawn at random and never trained:
$$\mathbf h(\mathbf x)=g\!\left(W\mathbf x+\mathbf b\right),$$
$$\hat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf h(\mathbf x)^{\top}\beta .$$
Only the output weights \(\beta\) are fitted, in closed form, on the \(N\) training rows stacked in \(H\in\mathbb R^{N\times L}\) and the targets \(Y\):
$$\beta=\left(H^{\top}H+\lambda I\right)^{-1}H^{\top}Y\quad(\text{ridge}),$$
$$\beta=H^{+}Y\quad(\lambda\to0,\ \text{Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse}).$$
Here \(g\) is the activation function, \(\lambda\ge0\) the ridge penalty and \(I\) the identity matrix. Training is one linear solve, so it takes seconds; several outputs share the same \(H\). Stored parameters for one output: \(dL+L+(L+1)\) (input weights, biases, output weights with intercept). ELM: Huang, Zhu and Siew (2006).
The fourteen ELM variants
They share \(H\) and differ only in the cost minimised to obtain \(\beta\): \(\min_\beta \sum_t \ell\!\left(y_t-\mathbf h_t^{\top}\beta\right)+R(\beta)\), with \(\ell\) the squared error (OLS, ridge), the absolute error (MAE), Huber, Welsch, \(|e|^3\), general \(|e|^p\), log-MSE, a Box-Cox target, a Gamma GLM or temporally correlated errors (Corr-ELM), and \(R\) a ridge, anisotropic Tikhonov or elastic-net penalty, or a robust risk.
Score against simple persistence
Errors are compared on the same samples with \(\mathrm{NICE}^{k}=L^k\text{-Error}_X/L^k\text{-Error}_P\), where \(L^k\text{-Error}=\big(\tfrac1n\sum|y-\hat y|^{k}\big)^{1/k}\) and P is simple persistence: 0 for a perfect forecast, 1 for persistence, > 1 worse than persistence (NICE guide).
How much model is enough
The capacity sweep plots \(\mathrm{NICE}^{\Sigma}\) against \(\log_{10}\) of the stored parameter count, from 5 to 1000 hidden neurons and several seeds. A model earns its size only if it moves down, not just right. A parameter count is not an energy measurement.
Models compared
Persistence baselines, including cyclic (one-day) persistence.
BLEND: convex combination of persistence and cyclic persistence, with the weight fitted by least squares or from a correlation formula.
AR-OLS: linear autoregression, fitted by pseudo-inverse.
ELM: one fixed random hidden layer, with only the output weights fitted. The 14 variants differ in their cost function or regularization: OLS, ridge, robust risk, anisotropic Tikhonov, Box-Cox target, MAE, log-MSE, Huber, L³, temporally correlated errors (Corr-ELM), elastic net, Welsch M-estimator, general Lᵖ and a Gamma GLM.
Ablations (a part removed to test its value): ELM without the cyclic time features.
TimeGPT, used without training on the site (zero-shot), as an optional foundation-model reference (needs an API key).
Capacity sweep
A dedicated run varies the hidden-layer size from 5 to 1000 neurons over several random seeds. It plots the error relative to simple persistence, NICE^Σ, against the logarithm of the stored parameter count, with AR-OLS and persistence as references. This is how the benchmark makes "how much model is enough" measurable rather than assumed.
Data
Palaiseau PV power at 30 min, from August 2020: shipped as a public example (data.zip), so the full benchmark runs end to end.
Other supported series, used in the research but not redistributed: PV plants (Oxelar, Signes, SOLETE, Alice Springs), GHI (Palaiseau, Alice Springs) and Barani MeteoHelix weather stations (temperature, pressure, humidity). Access goes through the data management plan on webservice-energy.org or the authors.
Any new site can be added by registering one entry in dataset_config.py. No model code changes.
Reproduce
Python 3.10 or later.
git clone https://github.com/cyrilvoyant/PV_ELM_pred.git
cd PV_ELM_pred
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
unzip data.zip
python scripts/run_full.py # all models, Palaiseau
DATASET=mysite python scripts/run_full.py # your own registered site
Running a single model script directly starts a fast 1000-point smoke test.
Good practice built into the pipeline
Input and target scaling are fitted on the training fold only. Since July 2026 the ELM target is centred as well, which removes a ridge bias on variables far from zero, such as pressure near 1013 hPa, without adding any fitted parameter.
Chronological splits, multiple random seeds, and separate daytime-only and all-hours scores.
Parameter counts are not energy measurements: report latency and memory separately, and never infer a carbon saving from a parameter count.
Status and scope
The associated manuscript on frugal, edge-oriented forecasting is in preparation. This page describes the public software only and reports no results from it. Rankings depend on the site, the horizon and the protocol. An endogenous short-term benchmark says nothing about weather-driven day-ahead forecasting without a separate test.
