URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/teaching/blend-worked-example.html
Title: BLEND persistence forecast: a worked example step by step
Language: en
Description: A numerical example of BLEND persistence with one least-squares weight per phase: past data only, explicit forecast origin, code results, sources and limits.

Worked example · fictitious teaching values · Published article, open code
BLEND persistence forecast: a worked example step by step
Principle 3 · Complexity only if it paysThe approachIn the story: the first level of the complexity ladder, computed by hand.
Worked example. All input values below are fictitious teaching values, not observations or results from the cited paper.
Result: with today’s 12:00 irradiance 600 W/m², yesterday’s 13:00 value 400 W/m² and a weight λ = 0.4 on the latest value, fitted on five past days, BLEND predicts 480 W/m² for 13:00.
The question
Should the next forecast follow the latest measurement or the recurring daily pattern? BLEND is a convex combination of both, persistence and cyclic persistence, with one weight per hour of the day. CLIPER, in the table below, is the convex combination of persistence and the mean. The forecast: Î(t+h) = (1 − λ)·I(t+h−T) + λ·I(t), as in the article. Here the weight is a one-line least-squares fit on past days.
The theory
With \(r=I(t)\) the latest value, \(c=I(t+h-T)\) the value at the target hour one cycle earlier and \(y=I(t+h)\) the value to forecast:
$$\hat I(t+h)=(1-\lambda)\,c+\lambda\,r,$$
$$\lambda=\frac{\sum (y-c)(r-c)}{\sum (r-c)^2}\ \text{on past days, clipped to }[0,1].$$
\(\lambda\) minimises \(\sum\big(y-c-\lambda(r-c)\big)^2\): a one-line least-squares fit, one weight per hour of the day. Full theory: BLEND guide.
Calculate it, without using the future
Set the forecast origin t to 12:00 today, horizon h to one hour and cycle T to 24 hours. The target is 13:00 today.
For each past day, note r = I(12:00), c = I(13:00 the day before) and y = I(13:00), the value that was to be forecast.
Fit the weight of the latest value: λ = Σ (y − c)(r − c) / Σ (r − c)² = 29,000 / 72,500 = 0.4. Keep λ between 0 and 1.
Today, r = 600 and c = 400: Î(13:00) = (1 − λ) c + λ r = 0.6 × 400 + 0.4 × 600 = 480 W/m².
Five fictitious past days, all at the 12:00 origin (W/m²)
Day | r = I(12:00) | c = I(13:00, day before) | y = I(13:00) | r − c | y − c |
Day −5 | 600 | 500 | 540 | 100 | 40 |
Day −4 | 550 | 650 | 610 | -100 | -40 |
Day −3 | 700 | 500 | 580 | 200 | 80 |
Day −2 | 450 | 550 | 510 | -100 | -40 |
Day −1 | 650 | 600 | 620 | 50 | 20 |
Fictitious comparison, same forecast target
Reference | Forecast W/m² |
Ordinary persistence | 600 |
Cyclic persistence (previous cycle, target phase) | 400 |
BLEND, least-squares weight | 480 |
Run it
The table above, in five lines (Python 3, NumPy; executed on 22 October 2026). The MATLAB implementation is predict_P_BLEND_LS.m in the repository.
import numpy as np
r = np.array([600, 550, 700, 450, 650]) # I(12:00) on five past days, W/m2
c = np.array([500, 650, 500, 550, 600]) # I(13:00) the day before
y = np.array([540, 610, 580, 510, 620]) # I(13:00), the value to forecast
lam = np.clip(np.sum((y - c) * (r - c)) / np.sum((r - c) ** 2), 0, 1)
print(lam, (1 - lam) * 400 + lam * 600)
Output:
0.4 480.0
What the code shows
Out-of-sample benchmark of the MATLAB repository (v1.1.1, synthetic signal, 10 realizations, nRMSE, lower is better):
Out-of-sample nRMSE by horizon (steps, T = 24), synthetic signal, day and night, mean of 10 realizations. x: the series; CS: the clear-sky reference, marked yes when the operator uses it. Lowest value per horizon in bold.Reference | CS | h = 1 | h = 2 | h = 3 | h = 6 | h = 9 |
CLIPER on the ratio to trend x/CS (clear-sky reference) | yes | 0.213 | 0.287 | 0.328 | 0.354 | 0.354 |
BLEND (one weight) on the ratio to trend x/CS (clear-sky reference) | yes | 0.219 | 0.303 | 0.359 | 0.413 | 0.398 |
Smart persistence, multiplicative | yes | 0.230 | 0.336 | 0.421 | 0.561 | 0.593 |
Stochastic persistence | yes | 0.260 | 0.388 | 0.470 | 0.474 | 0.468 |
CLIPER on the difference to trend x − μ(phase) (one weight) | | 0.223 | 0.299 | 0.337 | 0.354 | 0.354 |
CLIPER, weight per phase | | 0.263 | 0.323 | 0.345 | 0.354 | 0.354 |
BLEND, weight per phase (least squares) | | 0.302 | 0.398 | 0.445 | 0.488 | 0.495 |
BLEND, one weight, raw signal | | 0.365 | 0.457 | 0.484 | 0.498 | 0.499 |
BLEND, simplified weight per phase (1 + ρ)/2 | | 0.403 | 0.624 | 0.736 | 0.744 | 0.602 |
Cyclic persistence | | 0.502 | 0.502 | 0.502 | 0.502 | 0.502 |
All references and horizons: full results · CSV.
BLEND with a weight per phase improves on cyclic persistence at every horizon. Applying a reference to the ratio to trend x/CS (clear-sky reference) helps a lot on this signal: CLIPER on x/CS has the lowest mean errors, and stationary BLEND on x/CS is far better than BLEND on the raw signal. The simplified weight (1 + ρ)/2, also set for each phase, assumes the same mean at t and t + h; on a daily cycle it only helps at the first step.
What this study contributes
The published study develops a family of analytical forecasting operators for periodically correlated energy signals. The calculation illustrates its BLEND member; it does not reproduce the full benchmark of the article.
Limits that matter
A convex combination stays between its two inputs; this alone says nothing about forecast accuracy. The weight needs enough past cycles, changes with phase and horizon, and must not be fitted on the test period. Version 1.1.1 of the MATLAB code corrects errors of earlier versions and was audited independently.
Source definitions · MATLAB implementation (least-squares weight) · Full results table · Full method guide
Key point: weight the latest measurement (λ) and the same hour of the previous day (1 − λ), with one weight per hour fitted by least squares on past days. On the ratio to trend x/CS (the clear-sky index), persistence references become much stronger. A forecast and its observation must be aligned in time.
Authors, source and citation
Cyril Voyant, Candice Banes, Luis Garcia-Gutierrez, Gilles Notton, Milan Despotovic, Zaher Mundher Yaseen. Symmetry-constrained forecasting of periodically correlated energy processes. Applied Mathematical Modelling. doi:10.1016/j.apm.2026.116988 · BibTeX.
Cyril Voyant wrote this teaching page. The method belongs to the complete author team credited above.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/teaching/reference-model-comparison.html
Title: Persistence, AR and ELM compared on public PV data
Language: en
Description: Interactive Palaiseau teaching comparison with chronological holdout, identical forecast targets and explicit model costs.

Teaching demonstration · public data · open code
Persistence, AR and ELM compared on public PV data
Principle 3 · Complexity only if it paysThe approachIn the story: simple references compared on public data before any complex model.
Result first. One hour ahead, over the whole test period, the 30-neuron ELM lowers the RMSE of persistence by 17 % (1568 W against 1895 W), the six-lag linear model AR(6) by 15 % (1603 W), and the 10-neuron ELM is worse than persistence (2092 W). A bigger model is not automatically better, and a smaller one is not automatically enough.
Read this as a minimal baseline exercise
This demonstration deliberately uses only six raw-power lags. Unlike the author’s reference implementation, it omits target-time cyclic features and astronomical night masking. It can consequently predict positive PV power after sunset, especially at three hours. These results must not be used to characterize the performance of PV_ELM_pred or the associated research.
An independent audit found no target-time shift or RMSE arithmetic error. The protocol is too simple to showcase the full methods; the numbers are kept rather than replaced by models chosen after seeing their test errors.
At one hour, the displayed ELM-30 RMSE is 1.568 kW versus 1.895 kW for raw persistence (17.3% reduction). At three hours it is 2.698 kW, including avoidable nocturnal errors. These are whole-test errors, not errors for the plotted week. Further comparison should reproduce the reference preprocessing and report daytime/all-hours metrics separately.
Reference AR implementation · Reference cyclic features and night mask
New teaching calculation on an already-public dataset. These results are not the results of an unpublished manuscript, nor a reproduction of the full repository benchmark.
Does a larger model earn its extra complexity? Compare ordinary persistence, a six-lag linear model and two small Extreme Learning Machines on the same Palaiseau AC-power series.
Start with the evidence
Default horizon: one hour. RMSE below uses the entire held-out test period, day and night, with the same targets for every model. The chart shows only a selected week. Lower RMSE is better; model size is not an energy-consumption measurement.
One-hour test RMSE, W; seed 0 for ELMModel | RMSE W |
Persistence | 1895.3 |
AR(6) | 1602.7 |
ELM 10 | 2091.9 |
ELM 30 | 1568.4 |
Loading the interactive comparison… The static score table remains available without JavaScript.
The theory
Reference forecasts
At origin \(t\) and horizon \(h\), with cycle length \(T\) (24 hourly steps for a day):
$$\hat y^{\,\mathrm{P}}_{t+h}=y_t\quad(\text{persistence}),$$
$$\hat y^{\,\mathrm{C}}_{t+h}=y_{t+h-T}\quad(\text{cyclic persistence: same phase, previous cycle}).$$
AR(6) and ELM on six lags
Input \(\mathbf x_t=[y_t,\dots,y_{t-5}]\), standardised on the training part only.
$$\text{AR(6): }\ \hat y_{t+h}=a_0+\mathbf a^{\top}\mathbf x_t,$$
$$\text{ELM: }\ \hat y_{t+h}=\tanh\!\left(W\mathbf x_t+\mathbf b\right)^{\top}\beta+\beta_0,$$
with \(W,\mathbf b\) Gaussian random and fixed, and \((a_0,\mathbf a)\) and \(\beta\) fitted by ridge regression whose penalty is chosen on the validation part. Stored coefficients: \(7\) for AR(6), \(6L+L+(L+1)\) for an ELM with \(L\) neurons (81 for \(L=10\), 241 for \(L=30\)).
$$\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_{t}\left(y_{t+h}-\hat y_{t+h}\right)^2}\quad\text{on the whole test period, day and night.}$$
Protocol: keep the future out
Data: the public half-hour Palaiseau example in PV_ELM_pred/data.zip, with UTC timestamps and AC power in W.
Chronological split: first 60% training, next 20% validation, last 20% test. Split dates and a source checksum are in the downloadable JSON.
Six observations at or before forecast origin form the input. Standardization is estimated on training only. Each horizon is trained separately.
AR is linear ridge regression with an intercept. ELM uses fixed Gaussian random input weights and tanh activation; only output weights are fitted. Ridge penalty is selected on validation from a fixed grid.
Test targets never enter model fitting or penalty selection. Forecasts are clipped at zero. Night observations are retained; no filter uses the future observed production.
Size, variability and limits
AR stores 7 fitted coefficients. ELM-10 stores 81 coefficients (11 fitted); ELM-30 stores 241 (31 fitted), excluding scaling constants and runtime overhead. Three random ELM seeds are evaluated; the chart and table display seed 0. The downloadable report includes the three test errors. Do not select the best seed on test.
This is one site and one chronological split. Six lags and hidden sizes are fixed teaching choices. A daytime score, rolling evaluation, additional seasons and sites could change the conclusions. Persistence here means raw-power persistence; it is not smart persistence, BLEND or ARTU. Hardware energy and latency were not measured.
Reproduce and cite
Download observations, forecasts and protocol JSON · Download the calculation script (Python 3; install numpy, pandas and requests) · Public source dataset, original software and team credits.
ELM foundation: Guang-Bin Huang, Qin-Yu Zhu and Chee-Kheong Siew (2006), Extreme learning machine: Theory and applications. This page implements a small teaching model; it does not claim ELM’s invention or reproduce every PV_ELM_pred variant.
How to read it: compare methods on the same observations and the same horizon. The error shown covers the whole test, not only the week in the chart. A bigger model is not automatically better; this single calculation does not establish the general ranking of methods.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/teaching/solar-forecasting-basics.html
Title: Solar forecasting basics: a worked example on ten years of Ajaccio data
Language: en
Description: How to forecast solar irradiance one hour ahead, step by step: difference to trend, AR(1) and AR(p) by least squares, persistence references, error metrics…

Teaching · course material, Mines Paris – PSL
Solar forecasting basics: a worked example on ten years of Ajaccio data
Principle 2 · The model at the coreThe approachIn the story: understand the solar signal before any forecasting model.
The course and the stories on www.cyrilvoyant.com
The course, slide by slide: all 59 slides of the UE14 course with their text, outline and keyboard navigation; PowerPoint and PDF downloads.
Le cours en français: the same course in French, slide by slide.
Satellite forecasting: one cell or the whole field?: the story of how much space a satellite forecast needs, in plain words.
All research stories: the results behind the course, classified by step of the approach.
News: papers, software and essays, filterable by theme and year.
Cyril Voyant · Mines Paris – PSL · from the course UE14 (2026) · Published 2026-10-20
Result first. On ten years of hourly measurements in Ajaccio (Corsica), forecasting global irradiance one hour ahead, a linear AR(2) model with 2 coefficients reaches a daytime nRMSE of 21.3 %, smart persistence 22.0 %, and an Extreme Learning Machine with about 200 coefficients 20.5 %. Removing the solar cycle and choosing the right reference matter more than the model.
This page follows the course step by step, in English, with the actual numbers. It is meant for students and engineers who want the method, not only the vocabulary. Data: Météo-France, Ajaccio station, hourly global horizontal irradiance (GHI), 1998–2007.
1. Why forecast, and in which unit
PV output follows irradiance: P ≈ η · S · G. With P the power, S the module area, G the irradiance and a module efficiency η ≈ 20 %, 10 m² under 800 W/m² give about 1.6 kW. Forecasting GHI is therefore forecasting production. Grid operators need it to keep frequency stable, to charge or discharge storage at the right time, to schedule hydro or gas, and to sell energy at the best price.
A one-hour forecast lets the grid operator act before clouds arrive.
Irradiance is a power (W/m²); irradiation is an energy (Wh/m²). Hourly irradiation in Wh/m² equals the mean irradiance of that hour in W/m². Météo-France files give J/cm²: 1 J/cm² = 2.78 Wh/m², so Wh/m² = J/cm² / 0.36.
Hourly GHI measured at Ajaccio in 2007: 8,760 values, maximum 1,025 Wh/m², daytime mean 368 Wh/m² over 1998–2007.
Ten years are split chronologically: 1998–2005 to fit, 2006 to tune, 2007 to test, once, on data never seen.
2. Remove the solar cycle: the difference to trend
Raw GHI is not stationary: its mean depends on the hour and the month. A clear-sky model gives the irradiance without clouds; the course uses Solis (Ineichen, 2008), whose clear-sky error at Ajaccio is about 32 Wh/m². The difference to trend subtracts the clear-sky reference (the course denotes this difference CSI):
CSI(t) = GHI(t) − GHIcs(t) (≈ 0 under clear sky, 0 at night, negative under clouds)
Top: measured and clear-sky GHI on a clear, a variable and an overcast day. Bottom: the difference to trend; the daily cycle has gone.
Why a difference to trend rather than the ratio to trend GHI / GHIcs? The ratio is 0/0 at night and explodes near sunrise and sunset, so it requires filtering on solar elevation (for example above 10°). The difference works day and night with no filter. Its monthly mean stays between −105 and −43 Wh/m², against 163 to 521 Wh/m² for raw GHI: approximately stationary. It is then centred: y(t) = CSI(t) − μ, with μ ≈ −33 Wh/m².
3. How variable, how forecastable? sCV and F
The stochastic coefficient of variation (sCV) measures how far GHI departs from clear sky at a site; it does not depend on the horizon. Forecastability F adds the memory of clouds: F(h) = 1 − sCV · (1 − ρmax(h)), where ρmax(h) is the strongest remaining correlation of the difference to trend (sCV and F guide; Voyant et al., Renewable Energy 2026, doi:10.1016/j.renene.2025.123913 · BibTeX).
Ajaccio 1998–2007: sCV = 0.52 (fixed). F = 0.92 at 1 h, 0.74 at 3 h, 0.53 at 6 h: cloud memory fades within a few hours.
4. A first model, with numbers: AR(1)
y(t+1) = w · y(t) + ε(t+1), so the forecast h hours ahead is ŷ(t+h) = wh · y(t). At Ajaccio, w ≈ 0.84. A cloud gives CSI = −300 Wh/m², so y = −267. One hour later: 0.84 × (−267) = −224, i.e. a forecast CSI of −257 Wh/m², then −221 and −191 at 2 h and 3 h: the forecast returns towards the mean.
The forecast difference to trend returns towards its mean as the horizon grows.
5. AR(p) is a linear regression: least squares
With p lags, y = X w + ε, where each row of X holds the p previous values. Example with p = 2 and five centred values (−10, −25, −240, −180, −30): the rows are (−25, −10 → −240), (−240, −25 → −180), (−180, −240 → −30). The least-squares solution is exact, in one step: ŵ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy. At Ajaccio, AR(2) gives ŵ = (0.97, −0.15), computed in 6 ms on about 70,000 rows: the last value weighs by far the most.
How many lags? The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) suggests p ≈ 2 (PACF(1) = 0.84, PACF(2) = −0.15), but with 70,000 points almost everything is “significant”. The wrapper approach trains AR(p) for p = 1…12 and measures the validation error:
Validation RMSE (2006, daytime): 78.0 (p = 1), 77.7 (p = 2), 77.3 Wh/m² (p = 12). Parsimony: the smallest p within 0.5 % of the best, p = 2.
6. Always compare with a reference
A model that does not beat a simple reference brings nothing. Three references: simple persistence GHI(t+1) = GHI(t) (ignores the Sun's course); clear sky GHI(t+1) = GHIcs(t+1) (ignores clouds); smart persistence GHI(t+1) = GHI(t) − GHIcs(t) + GHIcs(t+1) (keeps the gap to clear sky; an AR(1) with w = 1). Two rules for every model: forecast 0 when the Sun is below the horizon, and replace negative forecasts by 0.
A variable day of 2007, 1-h forecasts: measurement, simple persistence, clear sky, smart persistence.
Errors: nMBE (bias, should stay below 1 % in magnitude), MAE, RMSE, nRMSE = RMSE / mean GHI. The skill score SS = 1 − RMSE / RMSE(smart persistence) compares with smart persistence; the NICEᵏ metrics compare with simple persistence on three error norms (Voyant et al., 2025, doi:10.1016/j.seta.2025.104588 · BibTeX).
Model (test 2007, 1 h) | RMSE day (W/m²) | nRMSE day | nRMSE day + night | SS | NICEΣ |
Simple persistence | 135 | 36.4 % | 51.5 % | −0.66 | 1.00 |
Clear sky | 148 | 39.9 % | 56.4 % | −0.82 | > 1 |
Smart persistence | 82 | 22.0 % | 31.0 % | 0.00 | 0.59 |
AR(2) | 79 | 21.3 % | 30.1 % | +0.03 | 0.58 |
ELM (L = 50, best draw) | 76 | 20.5 % | 28.9 % | +0.07 | 0.55 |
NICE: a useful forecast lies between 0 and 1; > 1 means worse than simple persistence. Smart persistence divides the RMSE of simple persistence by 1.7; AR(2) gains 3 % on it, the ELM 7 %. Daytime: 4,380 hours, mean GHI 372 W/m². Day + night: 8,759 hours, mean 186 W/m².
Day only or day + night? Adding night hours lowers the RMSE of AR(2) from 79 to 56 W/m² (everyone is right at night) but halves the mean (372 → 186), so the nRMSE rises from 21 % to 30 %. The ranking does not change; the numbers do. Always say which hours you used.
Four days of October 2007, 1-h forecasts: both models follow regular days and miss sudden changes, because an arriving cloud is not visible in the past.
7. Extreme Learning Machine: nonlinear, still least squares
An ELM is a one-hidden-layer network whose input weights and biases are drawn at random and frozen; only the output weights are fitted, by (ridge) least squares: H = g(X Win + b), β = (HᵀH + αI)⁻¹ Hᵀy (Huang et al., 2006), with X the inputs, Win and b the frozen weights and biases, g the activation function, L the number of neurons, α the ridge penalty and β the output weights. Same equation as AR, other columns. At Ajaccio, L = 50 neurons is enough (validation RMSE 85.2 at L = 5, 75.9 at L = 50, no gain beyond), and 20 random draws give a test nRMSE between 20.37 and 20.51 %.
ELM: random frozen input weights, output weights fitted by least squares.
Stationarize or give the time? A linear AR needs the difference to trend; an ELM given sin/cos encodings of hour and day can learn the solar cycle from raw GHI (Voyant et al., Solar Energy 2025, doi:10.1016/j.solener.2025.113490 · BibTeX).
Daytime nRMSE, test 2007: raw GHI, raw GHI + sin/cos, CSI, CSI + sin/cos, for AR(2) and ELM.
8. Online learning and frugality
With a sliding window, the model is re-estimated every hour on the last W hours (11 µs per update for AR, 38 µs for the ELM). AR(2) stays at 21.3–21.5 % even with one month of data; the ELM degrades to 25.6 % with one month: the more parameters, the more data a model needs.
Daytime nRMSE on 2007 as a function of the training window, from one month to eight years.
Model | Fitted coefficients | Training cost | Data needed | nRMSE day (test) |
Smart persistence | 0 | none | 1 hour | 22.0 % |
AR(2) | 2 | 6 ms | 1 month is enough | 21.3 % |
ELM (L = 50) | 51 (+150 random) | 58 ms per draw | several years | 20.5 % |
AR, 1-month sliding window | 2 | 11 µs per hour | 720 hours | 21.5 % |
Timings on a laptop; only orders of magnitude matter. The right question is not “which model is best?” but “does the gain justify the cost?” in computation, data, maintenance and monitoring. See also the PV_ELM_pred benchmark and persistence and BLEND.
Takeaways
A forecast is useful only if it beats a reference: always report persistence and smart persistence.
Remove or encode the solar cycle before learning, and say how (difference, ratio or time encoding).
Choose model complexity on data you do not test on; state day-only or day + night.
A small model refreshed often can rival a larger one: frugality is a design choice.
Questions and answers
How do you forecast solar irradiance one hour ahead?
Remove the deterministic solar cycle with a clear-sky model (here Solis), forecast the difference to trend with a linear autoregressive model fitted by least squares, add the clear-sky irradiance back, and compare the result with smart persistence. On ten years of Ajaccio data, AR(2) reaches a daytime nRMSE of 21.3 % at 1 h, against 22.0 % for smart persistence.
Difference to trend or ratio to trend: which should I use?
Both aim to remove the deterministic solar cycle; neither guarantees stationarity. The difference to trend CSI = GHI − GHIcs (in W/m²) is defined day and night (0 − 0 = 0) and needs no solar-elevation filter. The ratio to trend GHI / GHIcs is unitless and common in the literature, but undefined at night and unstable near sunrise and sunset, so it needs a filter such as solar elevation above 10°.
What is smart persistence in solar forecasting?
Smart (clear-sky) persistence assumes the sky stays the same: it keeps the current gap to the clear-sky irradiance, GHI(t+1) = GHI(t) − GHIcs(t) + GHIcs(t+1). It is an AR(1) with weight 1 and the reference of the skill score. At Ajaccio it divides the RMSE of simple persistence by about 1.7.
Why must forecast errors state day-only or day-and-night hours?
At night every model predicts zero and is right, so adding night hours lowers the RMSE (79 → 56 W/m² for AR(2) at Ajaccio) but halves the mean irradiance (372 → 186 W/m²), which raises the nRMSE (21 % → 30 %). The ranking of models does not change, but the numbers do.
Is an Extreme Learning Machine worth it over a linear AR model?
At Ajaccio, 1 h ahead, an ELM with 50 hidden neurons reaches 20.5 % daytime nRMSE against 21.3 % for AR(2): about 4 points of skill score for roughly 100 times more coefficients, a result that depends on the random draw, and several years of training data. The useful question is whether the gain justifies the cost.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/teaching/solar-forecasting-course.html
Title: Forecasting the intermittent solar resource: a course
Language: en
Description: Course by Cyril Voyant (Mines Paris – PSL): solar radiation, clear-sky index, AR models, NICE metrics, Extreme Learning Machines, online learning, frugal AI.

Forecasting the intermittent solar resource: a course
Principle 2 · The model at the coreThe approachIn the story: understand the solar signal first, then climb the ladder of models one level at a time, and only as far as it pays.

Course UE14, Mines Paris – PSL, 2026 · taught in French · slides and Python/Matlab practicals
How do you forecast solar irradiance one hour ahead, and how do you know whether your forecast is any good? This course answers both questions from scratch, on ten years of real hourly measurements from Ajaccio (Corsica, 1998–2007), and ends with the methods used in current research: difference to trend and ratio to trend, forecastability, NICE metrics, Extreme Learning Machines, online learning and frugal AI.
In English: Solar forecasting basics: a worked example on ten years of Ajaccio data, the whole course step by step with the real numbers.
Questions answered in the course
How do you forecast solar irradiance one hour ahead?
Start by removing the deterministic solar cycle with a clear-sky model: the course uses the difference to trend (GHI: global horizontal irradiance; cs: clear sky), CSI = GHI − GHIcs (a ratio to trend GHI / GHIcs is the other common choice), then centres it. Fit an autoregressive model AR(p) on it by ordinary least squares, choosing the order p on data not used for testing (autocorrelation ACF, partial autocorrelation PACF, information criteria AIC/BIC). Compare it with persistence and smart persistence, and add a nonlinear model such as an Extreme Learning Machine only if it beats them. The methods are reviewed in Voyant et al., Renewable Energy 2017 (doi:10.1016/j.renene.2016.12.095 · BibTeX) and benchmarked in Voyant et al., Renewable Energy 2022 (doi:10.1016/j.renene.2022.04.065 · BibTeX).
What are difference to trend and ratio to trend in solar forecasting?
Compare measured global horizontal irradiance with the clear-sky reference at the same place and time: use a difference to trend (CSI = GHI − GHIcs, used in the course: about 0 under clear sky, negative under clouds) or a ratio to trend (GHI / GHIcs). It removes most of the daily and annual cycle, so that statistical models work on the cloud-driven part. The choice of clear-sky model matters for short-term forecasts (Voyant et al., Solar Energy 2025, doi:10.1016/j.solener.2025.113490 · BibTeX).
How do you know whether a solar forecast is good?
Compare it with reference forecasts on the same samples: persistence and smart (clear-sky) persistence at least. Report normalized bias (nMBE) and error (nRMSE), a skill score against the reference, or the persistence-normalized NICEᵏ metrics, and say whether night hours are included.
How variable and forecastable is solar irradiance at a site?
The course measures site variability with the stochastic coefficient of variation (sCV) and a forecastability index F, introduced in Voyant et al., Renewable Energy 2026 (doi:10.1016/j.renene.2025.123913 · BibTeX). They help compare sites before comparing forecasting models.
Course outline
Why forecast solar power? Grid integration, irradiance vs irradiation vs PV output, the Ajaccio dataset.
Solar radiation: direct and diffuse components, attenuation in the atmosphere, sun position, the double (daily and annual) seasonality of GHI.
Time series and forecasting: components and decomposition, horizons and time steps, predictable part vs error, a worked AR(1) example.
Clear sky: difference to trend and ratio to trend: the Solis clear-sky model, two ways to stationarize (difference or ratio), is the CSI stationary?, site variability with the stochastic coefficient of variation (sCV) and forecastability F, step-by-step preprocessing.
Autoregressive models and least squares: from AR(p) to linear regression, building X and y by hand, ordinary least squares and its geometric meaning, train/validation/test split, choosing p with ACF, PACF, filter or wrapper approaches, AIC/BIC.
Evaluation, ELM and online learning: reference models (persistence, smart persistence), nMBE, nRMSE, skill score and NICEΣ, day-only vs day-and-night scores, Extreme Learning Machines (principle, neurons, random draws, sin/cos time encoding), AR vs ELM, sliding-window online learning, frugality.
What students take away
A forecast is only useful if it beats a reference: always report persistence and smart persistence.
Remove or encode the deterministic solar cycle before learning, and state how (difference, ratio, or time encoding).
Choose model complexity from data you have not tested on; report the protocol (day only or day and night).
A smaller model that is refreshed often can rival a larger one: frugality is a design choice.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/teaching/stochastic-persistence-worked-example.html
Title: Stochastic persistence for solar nowcasting: a worked example
Language: en
Description: Additive and multiplicative stochastic persistence explained with a three-observation example, source equations and practical limits.

Worked example · fictitious teaching values · Published article
Stochastic persistence for solar nowcasting: a worked example
Principle 3 · Complexity only if it paysThe approachIn the story: a clear-sky reference, computed by hand, simple and hard to beat.
Stochastic persistence: why average the clear-sky gap?
Worked example. All input values below are fictitious teaching values, not observations or results from the cited paper.
Result: three fictitious observations give an additive stochastic-persistence forecast of 510 W/m². The multiplicative form gives 497.97 W/m². They are different models.
Why average before persisting?
A single measurement carries useful recent information and fluctuations. The idea is to persist a short-window summary relative to clear sky rather than copy every fluctuation. “Stochastic” here does not mean adding a random draw to the forecast.
Three past observations
Fictitious daylight inputs, oldest to newestTime | GHI W/m² | CS W/m² | CS−GHI | GHI/CS |
t−2 | 400 | 500 | 100 | 0.80 |
t−1 | 450 | 600 | 150 | 0.75 |
t | 480 | 800 | 320 | 0.60 |
The theory
Over the last \(N\) available observations, persist a short-window summary of the departure from clear sky instead of the last value (Voyant and Notton, 2018, Eqs. 5–11):
$$\text{additive: }\ \widehat{\mathrm{GHI}}(t+h)=\mathrm{CS}(t+h)-\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\Big(\mathrm{CS}(t-i)-\mathrm{GHI}(t-i)\Big),$$
$$\text{multiplicative: }\ \widehat{\mathrm{GHI}}(t+h)=\mathrm{CS}(t+h)\left(\prod_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{\mathrm{GHI}(t-i)}{\mathrm{CS}(t-i)}\right)^{1/N}.$$
The first averages the deficit arithmetically, the second the ratio geometrically: they are different models. \(N=1\) gives back the usual clear-sky persistences. \(N\) is chosen on a validation period.
Additive form, step by step
Equation 5 of Voyant and Notton (2018) uses the mean deficit Δ = CS − GHI (the difference to trend with its sign reversed; GHI: global horizontal irradiance, CS: clear-sky irradiance) over the last N available observations. With N = 3, Δ̄ = (100+150+320)/3 = 190 W/m². Given CS(t+h) = 700 W/m², forecast GHI = 700−190 = 510 W/m². Equivalently: mean(GHI) + future CS − mean(CS).
Multiplicative form
The other form uses the geometric mean of the ratios to trend GHI/CS: (0.80 × 0.75 × 0.60)^(1/3) ≈ 0.711379. Multiplying by future clear sky 700 gives 497.97 W/m². An arithmetic mean of these ratios to trend would implement a different rule.
Run it
Python 3, NumPy; executed on 22 October 2026.
import numpy as np
ghi = np.array([400, 450, 480]); cs = np.array([500, 600, 800]); cs_future = 700
print(cs_future - np.mean(cs - ghi)) # additive
print(round(cs_future * np.prod(ghi / cs) ** (1 / 3), 2)) # multiplicative
Output:
510.0
497.97
Compare without claiming a winner
Ordinary persistence predicts 480 W/m². With N = 1, the additive clear-sky correction predicts 700−320 = 380 W/m²; persistence of the ratio to trend predicts 0.60 × 700 = 420 W/m². A held-out observation is needed to rank these forecasts.
What this study contributes
Voyant and Notton develop additive and multiplicative stochastic-persistence forecasts using short-window summaries relative to clear sky. The source provides the definitions, evaluation conditions and selection of the window length.
Limits and reproducibility
Averaging can suppress useful rapid changes as well as noise. Choose N on a validation period, then keep the test period untouched. Ratios to trend near zero clear sky need filtering; geometric means need an explicit policy for zero or invalid values. The example contains only positive daylight values. Any physical clipping must be reported. It proves the arithmetic, not superiority at a real station.
Author manuscript on HAL, equations 5–11 · Author’s public code (no dedicated implementation of this paper is asserted).
Key point: smooth the deviation from clear sky before extending it. Do not confuse the arithmetic mean of the deficit with the geometric mean of the ratio; the window size remains to be validated.
Authors, source and citation
Cyril Voyant, Gilles Notton. Solar irradiation nowcasting by stochastic persistence: A new parsimonious, simple and efficient forecasting tool. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews. doi:10.1016/j.rser.2018.04.116 · BibTeX.
Cyril Voyant wrote this teaching page. The method belongs to the complete author team credited above.

Title: LQL-Equiv: free online EQD2, BED, NTCP and TCP calculator for radiotherapy
Language: en
Description: Free browser calculator for EQD2, BED, NTCP, TCP and cancer risk under the LQL model. Validated on 4,438 schedules. Research and education only.

LQL-Equiv: free online EQD2, BED, NTCP and TCP calculator for radiotherapy
Principle 2 · The model at the coreThe approachIn the story: when the link is known, compute it directly. No data and no AI are needed: the linear-quadratic-linear model gives the equivalent dose, checked against the 2014 version on 4,438 schedules.
In brief
LQL-Equiv computes biologically effective doses (BED), equivalent doses (EQD2), NTCP and TCP under the linear-quadratic-linear model, for 34 organs at risk and 20 tumour sites, in the browser.
Version 3.0 reproduces the 2014 MATLAB software on 4,438 treatment schedules: 69,125 of 69,131 values agree.
C. Voyant and D. Julian, SoftwareX 36, 103085 (2026), doi:10.1016/j.softx.2026.103085; for research and teaching only, not a medical device.
Cyril Voyant · Updated 2026-10-18
Open the calculator
Free, no installation. Runs entirely in your browser: nothing you enter leaves the page.
Biologically equivalent doses in radiotherapy, under the linear-quadratic-linear model. LQL-Equiv computes the biologically effective dose (BED), the equivalent dose in a reference fractionation (EQD2 and others), the normal-tissue complication probability (NTCP), the tumour control probability (TCP) and the radiation-induced cancer risk. It handles successive treatment courses separated by gaps, two fractions a day, accelerated proliferation and overall treatment time.
For research and education only. Not a medical device. Outputs must not be used to choose or modify a prescription, to compensate a real interruption, to sum dose for a reirradiation decision, or to predict a probability for an individual patient. NTCP and TCP are model illustrations that have never been validated against clinical outcome.
The theory
Direct calculation. The link between a fractionation schedule and its biological effect is given by an explicit model, so it is computed, not learned. No data and no AI are needed: this work stops at the first rung of the complexity ladder.
Where LQL-Equiv sits on the complexity ladder: direct calculation. PDF
Definitions
\(n,\ d\)
number of fractions and dose per fraction (Gy)
\(\alpha/\beta\)
tissue parameter of the linear-quadratic model (Gy)
\(d_T\)
transition dose above which the response becomes linear (Gy)
\(\gamma/\alpha\)
slope of the linear tail (library value 5)
\(T,\ T_k,\ T_p\)
overall time, kick-off time and potential doubling time of the tumour (days)
\(T_{1/2}\)
repair half-time of the tissue; \(\phi\) follows from it
\(TD_{50},\ m\)
dose giving 50 % complications and slope parameter of the Lyman model
\(TCD_{50},\ \gamma_{50}\)
dose giving 50 % tumour control and normalized slope of the curve at that dose
Biologically effective dose
Linear-quadratic (LQ), for \(d\lt d_T\):
$$\mathrm{BED}=n\,d\left(1+\frac{d}{\alpha/\beta}\right).$$
Linear-quadratic-linear (LQL, Astrahan), for \(d\ge d_T\): the curve continues as a straight line, which avoids the unbounded growth of LQ at high dose per fraction:
$$\mathrm{BED}=n\left[d_T\left(1+\frac{d_T}{\alpha/\beta}\right)+\frac{\gamma}{\alpha}\,(d-d_T)\right].$$
Two fractions a day, 6 h apart: the quadratic term is multiplied by \(1+H_2\) (Thames incomplete repair), \(H_2=\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}\left(2-\frac{1-\phi^2}{1-\phi}\right)\), \(\phi=e^{-0.693\cdot6/T_{1/2}}\). Tumour repopulation removes \(\frac{\ln2}{\alpha T_p}\,(T-T_k)\) Gy when \(T\gt T_k\).
Equivalent dose
\(\mathrm{EQD}_{x}\) is the total dose in fractions of \(x\) Gy (2 Gy for EQD2) that gives the same BED; without time correction and for \(x\lt d_T\):
$$\mathrm{EQD}_x=\frac{\mathrm{BED}}{1+x/(\alpha/\beta)}.$$
With overall time, LQL-Equiv solves for the number of reference fractions numerically.
Model illustrations (never clinically validated)
$$\mathrm{NTCP}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{EQD}-TD_{50}}{m\,TD_{50}}\right)\quad\text{(Lyman, }\Phi\text{ the standard normal distribution)},$$
$$\mathrm{TCP}=\frac{1}{1+\left(TCD_{50}/\mathrm{EQD}\right)^{4\gamma_{50}}}\quad\text{(logistic)},$$
or, with the Poisson form,
$$\mathrm{TCP}=2^{-\exp\left(e\gamma_{50}\left(1-\mathrm{EQD}/TCD_{50}\right)\right)}.$$
Worked example: one fraction of 15 Gy to the rectum
Rectum: \(\alpha/\beta=3.9\) Gy, \(d_T=7.8\) Gy. LQ: \(15\,(1+15/3.9)=72.7\) Gy. LQL: \(7.8\,(1+7.8/3.9)+5\,(15-7.8)=23.4+36.0=59.4\) Gy, 18 % lower. The difference grows with the dose per fraction, which is why the choice of model matters when comparing hypofractionated and conventional schedules. The calculator then adds the time and repair corrections of the tissue.
LQ and LQL for the rectum (α/β = 3.9 Gy, dT = 7.8 Gy), computed with the library of LQL-Equiv. PDF
Try it in your browser
BED under LQ and LQL, dose per fraction by dose per fraction. Move the slider past the transition dose to see where the linear-quadratic model overestimates.
Run it
The core package depends only on the Python standard library. Executed on 22 October 2026 (Python 3.12). Fictitious research case; not a medical device.
# pip install -e . (from a clone of github.com/cyrilvoyant/LQL-Equiv-web)
from lqlequiv import Course, Prescription, compute, load_library
library = load_library()
plan = Prescription(courses=(Course(dose_per_fraction=2.0, n_fractions=39),), reference_dose=2.0)
result = compute(library.organ("Rectum"), library.tumour_site("Prostate"), plan)
print(f"BED {result.courses[0].bed_oar:.1f} Gy, EQD2 {result.eqd_oar_total:.1f} Gy, NTCP {result.ntcp_percent:.1f} %")
Output:
BED 102.1 Gy, EQD2 78.0 Gy, NTCP 43.4 %
Validated against the original, case by case
Version 3.0 is a complete reimplementation of the 2014 MATLAB application. The 2014 software was run over 4,438 treatment schedules: every organ/tumour pair, a wide fractionation grid, gaps, twice-daily schedules and random multi-course plans.
|
|
Values compared |
69,131 |
Agreeing at the 2014 output precision |
69,125 (99.991%) |
Cases differing |
2 of 4,438, both exact ties of the 2014 search grid |
Sixteen analytical checks that do not rely on the 2014 code (continuity at the transition dose, EQD = n·d at the reference fraction size, additivity, round trip) test whether the calculation itself is right. One of them revealed the only change that moves a number: overall time is now counted once instead of twice. The 2014 behavior stays available for recomputing older results.
Questions about EQD2, BED and LQL-Equiv
How do I calculate EQD2 online?
Open LQL-Equiv, a free calculator that runs entirely in the browser (nothing entered leaves the page). Enter the dose per fraction, the number of fractions and the organ at risk or tumour site; it returns the BED, the EQD2 and, as model illustrations, NTCP and TCP. It is for research and education only, not a medical device.
What is the difference between BED and EQD2?
Under the linear-quadratic model, the biologically effective dose is BED = n·d·(1 + d/(α/β)) for n fractions of dose d. EQD2 is the total dose in 2 Gy fractions that gives the same BED: EQD2 = BED / (1 + 2/(α/β)). BED is an abstract quantity; EQD2 is expressed in clinically familiar 2 Gy-equivalent terms. LQL-Equiv adds a linear tail above a transition dose and can include overall treatment time.
Why use a linear-quadratic-linear (LQL) model?
The pure linear-quadratic model keeps curving upward at high dose per fraction. The LQL variant used in LQL-Equiv switches to a linear dose response above a transition dose, which matters when comparing hypofractionated and conventional schedules. The choice of model and parameters remains an assumption to state explicitly.
Can LQL-Equiv be used for treatment decisions?
No. It is for research and education only and is not a medical device. Its outputs must not be used to choose or modify a prescription, compensate a real interruption, sum dose for a reirradiation decision or predict a probability for an individual patient; NTCP and TCP have never been validated against clinical outcome.
What it covers
34 organs at risk and 20 tumour sites, each parameter with its documented provenance.
Linear-quadratic model with a linear tail above the transition dose; Dale and Van Dyk proliferation; Thames incomplete-repair correction; Lyman NTCP; logistic or Poisson TCP; linear-exponential cancer risk.
Also a Python library with no dependency beyond the standard library: pip install -e ., then compute(...).
Typical uses in teaching and research
Show students how EQD2 depends on dose per fraction and on α/β.
Compare hypofractionated and conventional schedules on the same organ.
Explore how a treatment gap changes the equivalent dose under the model's assumptions.

URL: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/tools/tunnel-load-simulator-fr.html
Title: Tunnel Load Simulator : consommation électrique des tunnels routiers, application web Monte Carlo
Language: fr
Other language: en: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/tools/tunnel-load-simulator.html
Description: Simulateur Monte Carlo de la consommation électrique des tunnels routiers : trafic, ventilation, éclairage, aléas, enveloppes P10–P90, export CSV.

Tunnel Load Simulator : consommation électrique des tunnels routiers, application web Monte Carlo
Principe 2 · Le modèle au cœur Voir l’approcheDans le récit : aucune mesure n’existe, la consommation est donc simulée à partir de ce que l’on sait, de façon simple, explicite et avec ses limites énoncées ; une année au pas de 10 minutes en environ 150 ms.
En bref
Le Tunnel Load Simulator génère la consommation électrique d’un tunnel routier à partir de sa géométrie, de son trafic, de son éclairage et de sa ventilation, avec des épisodes aléatoires de pollution et d’accident.
Une année au pas de 10 minutes se simule en environ 150 ms ; des tirages Monte Carlo (la même simulation répétée avec des aléas différents) donnent les médianes et les enveloppes P10–P90 de l’énergie, de la puissance de pointe et du facteur de charge (définition de P10–P90).
H. El-Houari et C. Voyant, SoftwareX 35, 102946 (2026), doi:10.1016/j.softx.2026.102946 ; un générateur de premier ordre, à calibrer sur des mesures avant tout usage d’ingénierie.
Cyril Voyant · Mis à jour le 2026-11-03 · version française de la page anglaise
Ouvrir le simulateur
Hébergement gratuit : l’application peut mettre environ une minute à se réveiller lors de la première visite (interface en anglais).
Le récit de recherche : Simuler ce que l’on ne peut pas encore mesurer : la consommation électrique des tunnels routiers.
Quelle quantité d’électricité un tunnel routier consomme-t-il, et avec quelle incertitude ? Le Tunnel Load Simulator génère des séries temporelles réalistes de puissance et d’énergie à partir de la géométrie du tunnel, de son contexte d’exploitation, de la ventilation pilotée par le trafic, du régime d’éclairage et de perturbations aléatoires, comme les épisodes de pollution et les accidents. Il lance N réalisations Monte Carlo indépendantes (une réalisation est une simulation complète d’une année) et renvoie la médiane, le P10 et le P90 des principaux indicateurs, avec une enveloppe d’incertitude sur la série temporelle.
Rapide : le moteur est entièrement vectorisé (il calcule sur des tableaux entiers plutôt que pas à pas). Une année au pas de 10 minutes se simule en environ 150 ms ; 20 réalisations Monte Carlo en environ 0,6 s.
La théorie
Simuler à partir de ce que l’on sait. Aucune mesure du tunnel n’existe : la consommation est donc construite à partir de ce que l’on sait de sa géométrie, de son trafic, de son éclairage et de sa ventilation, avec des perturbations aléatoires explicites. Aucune donnée n’est nécessaire, et aucune n’est inventée : le modèle est simple, ses paramètres sont visibles et ses limites sont énoncées.
Place du Tunnel Load Simulator sur l’échelle de complexité : la simulation à partir de ce que l’on sait. PDF
La consommation, terme par terme
À chaque pas de 10 minutes \(t\), la puissance est la somme de quatre termes, affectée d’un bruit multiplicatif :
$$P(t)=\max\!\Big(0,\ \big[P_0+P_{\mathrm{light}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{vent}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{aux}}(t)\big]\big(1+\varepsilon_t\big)\Big),$$
$$\varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).$$
Ici \(P_0\) est la base fixe, \(P_{\mathrm{light}}\) l’éclairage, \(P_{\mathrm{vent}}\) la ventilation, \(P_{\mathrm{aux}}\) les auxiliaires, et \(\varepsilon_t\) un bruit gaussien (loi normale) de moyenne nulle et d’écart-type \(\sigma\). Les grandeurs \(L_{\mathrm{km}}\), \(n_{\mathrm{lanes}}\) et \(n_{\mathrm{tubes}}\) ci-dessous sont la longueur du tunnel en kilomètres, le nombre de voies et le nombre de tubes.
Trafic \(q(t)\)
plancher nocturne \(0.16+0.06\cos\frac{2\pi(\tau-3)}{24}\) (\(\tau\) : heure de la journée) plus des pics gaussiens le matin et le soir, normalisés par une journée de référence, puis multipliés par le contexte (urbain 1,20, périurbain 1,00, rural 0,78), la saison (hiver 1,12 … été 0,92), le jour de la semaine (jours ouvrés 1,00, samedi 0,86, dimanche 0,78), le niveau de trafic et un facteur aléatoire journalier ; borné à \([0,2]\)
Éclairage
\(P_{\mathrm{light}}=p_\ell\,L_{\mathrm{km}}\,n_{\mathrm{lanes}}\,\min\!\big(1,\ f_{\min}+(1-f_{\min})(1-D(t))+c_q\,q(t)\big)\), où \(D(t)\) est un indicateur lisse de lumière du jour construit à partir du lever et du coucher du soleil selon la saison, et où \((p_\ell,c_q,f_{\min})\) (puissance par kilomètre et par voie, sensibilité au trafic, fraction minimale de puissance) dépendent de la technologie (LED adaptative, c’est-à-dire dont l’intensité suit la lumière du jour et le trafic : 16 kW/km/voie, 0,18, 0,20)
Ventilation
\(P_{\mathrm{vent}}=p_v\,L_{\mathrm{km}}\,n_{\mathrm{tubes}}\,\big(0.15+s\,q(t)\big)\,a\,g\,\big(1+s_p\,\mathbb 1_{\mathrm{pollution}}(t)+s_a\,\mathbb 1_{\mathrm{accident}}(t)\big)\), où \(p_v\) dépend du système (longitudinal, c’est-à-dire où l’air est poussé le long du tunnel : 120 kW/km/tube), \(s\) est la sensibilité au trafic, \(s_p\) et \(s_a\) les majorations en cas de pollution et d’accident (les indicatrices \(\mathbb 1\) valent 1 pendant l’épisode et 0 sinon), le facteur d’altitude est \(a=1+\max(z-500,0)/6000\) (\(z\) : altitude) et le facteur de pente \(g=1+|i|/20\) (\(i\) : pente)
Auxiliaires
\(P_{\mathrm{aux}}=p_a\,L_{\mathrm{km}}\,n_{\mathrm{tubes}}\,(1+\min(z_{\max},800)/6000)\,(1+\eta_t)\), \(\eta_t\sim\mathcal N(0,0.025^2)\), où \(p_a\) est la puissance linéique des auxiliaires et \(z_{\max}\) l’altitude maximale
Événements
épisodes de pollution et accidents tirés chaque jour avec des probabilités, des heures de début et des durées données
Construction de la consommation : un jour ouvré, une réalisation, de l’exemple public. PDF
Monte Carlo et indicateurs
\(R\) réalisations indépendantes (graines \(42,43,\dots\), c’est-à-dire les valeurs initiales du générateur aléatoire) donnent la distribution de chaque indicateur ; l’enveloppe reporte la médiane et la bande P10–P90. Le P10 est la valeur sous laquelle se trouvent 10 % des réalisations, le P90 celle sous laquelle se trouvent 90 % d’entre elles, et la médiane (P50) sépare les réalisations en deux moitiés : la bande P10–P90 contient donc les 80 % centrales. Énergie annuelle \(E=\sum_t P(t)\,\Delta t\) (\(\Delta t\) : pas de temps) ; facteur de charge \(\bar P/P_{\max}\) (puissance moyenne sur puissance de pointe) ; consommation spécifique \(E/\text{longueur}\).
Hypothèses et validité
Un générateur synthétique de premier ordre : les coefficients sont des ordres de grandeur d’ingénierie, pas des mesures. Adapté au prototypage, à l’enseignement et aux études de sensibilité de pré-dimensionnement ; à calibrer sur des données mesurées avant tout usage d’ingénierie.
Lancer l’exemple
L’exemple public : un tunnel périurbain de 1,5 km, deux tubes de deux voies, éclairage LED adaptatif, ventilation longitudinale, une année au pas de 10 minutes, 20 réalisations. Le paquet se trouve dans src/, d’où PYTHONPATH=src. Exécuté le 22 octobre 2026 (Python 3.12).
git clone https://github.com/cyrilvoyant/tunnel-load-simulator.git
cd tunnel-load-simulator
pip install -r requirements.txt
PYTHONPATH=src python examples/monte_carlo_example.py # PowerShell: $env:PYTHONPATH="src"; python examples/monte_carlo_example.py
Sortie du programme (en anglais, telle qu’il l’affiche ; energy = énergie, peak power = puissance de pointe) :
=== Monte Carlo results (20 runs) ===
Annual energy (MWh):
Median : 3233.4
P10 : 3229.5
P90 : 3237.1
Peak power (kW):
Median : 873.4
P10 : 792.2
P90 : 922.2
Autres médianes de la même exécution : puissance moyenne 369 kW, facteur de charge 0,42, consommation spécifique 2 156 kWh par mètre et par an.
Une semaine de l’exemple public : médiane et bande P10–P90 sur 20 réalisations. PDF
Ce que l’on obtient
Énergie annuelle (MWh), puissance de pointe et puissance moyenne (kW), facteur de charge, consommation spécifique (kWh/m/an) et nombre d’événements, pour chaque réalisation et sous forme de distributions.
Graphiques interactifs et export CSV (fichier lisible dans un tableur) des séries temporelles.
Un paquet Python utilisable sans l’interface (run_monte_carlo(...)), avec des exemples et des tests.
Usages typiques
Études de sensibilité de pré-dimensionnement : technologie d’éclairage, type de ventilation, niveau de trafic.
Profils de consommation synthétiques pour la recherche sur la gestion de l’énergie et l’intégration des énergies renouvelables dans les tunnels.
Enseigner l’incertitude Monte Carlo sur un cas d’ingénierie.
Statut : générateur synthétique de premier ordre, adapté au prototypage, aux démonstrations et aux études de sensibilité de pré-dimensionnement. À calibrer sur des données mesurées avant tout usage d’ingénierie ou de publication.

Title: Tunnel Load Simulator: electricity demand of road tunnels, Monte Carlo web app
Language: en
Other language: fr: https://cyrilvoyant.github.io/tools/tunnel-load-simulator-fr.html
Description: Monte Carlo electricity demand of road tunnels: traffic, ventilation, lighting, random events, P10–P90 envelopes, CSV export. Free web app.

Tunnel Load Simulator: electricity demand of road tunnels, Monte Carlo web app
Principle 2 · The model at the coreThe approachIn the story: no measurements exist, so the load is simulated from what is known, simple, explicit, with its limits stated; one year at 10-minute resolution in about 150 ms.
In brief
The Tunnel Load Simulator generates the electricity demand of a road tunnel from its geometry, traffic, lighting and ventilation, with random pollution episodes and accidents.
One year at 10-minute resolution runs in about 150 ms; Monte Carlo runs give medians and P10-P90 envelopes of energy, peak power and load factor.
H. El-Houari and C. Voyant, SoftwareX 35, 102946 (2026), doi:10.1016/j.softx.2026.102946; a first-order generator, to calibrate on measurements before engineering use.
Cyril Voyant · Updated 2026-10-18 · Version française
Open the simulator
Free hosting: the app may take about a minute to wake up on first visit.
How much electricity does a road tunnel use, and how uncertain is it? The Tunnel Load Simulator generates realistic time series of power and energy demand from the tunnel's geometry, operating context, traffic-driven ventilation, lighting regime and random disturbances such as pollution episodes and accidents. It runs N independent Monte Carlo realizations and returns median, P10 and P90 values of the key indicators, with an uncertainty envelope on the time series.
Fast: the engine is fully vectorized. One year at 10-minute resolution simulates in about 150 ms; 20 Monte Carlo runs in about 0.6 s.
The theory
Simulation from what is known. No measurements of the tunnel exist, so the load is built from what is known about its geometry, traffic, lighting and ventilation, with explicit random disturbances. No data are needed, and none are faked: the model is simple, its parameters are visible, and its limits are stated.
Where the Tunnel Load Simulator sits on the complexity ladder: simulation from what is known. PDF
The load, term by term
At each 10-minute step \(t\), the power is the sum of four terms with a multiplicative noise:
$$P(t)=\max\!\Big(0,\ \big[P_0+P_{\mathrm{light}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{vent}}(t)+P_{\mathrm{aux}}(t)\big]\big(1+\varepsilon_t\big)\Big),$$
$$\varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).$$
Traffic \(q(t)\)
night floor \(0.16+0.06\cos\frac{2\pi(\tau-3)}{24}\) plus Gaussian morning and evening peaks, normalised by a one-day reference, then multiplied by context (urban 1.20, peri-urban 1.00, rural 0.78), season (winter 1.12 … summer 0.92), day of week (weekdays 1.00, Saturday 0.86, Sunday 0.78), traffic level and a daily random factor; clipped to \([0,2]\)
Lighting
\(P_{\mathrm{light}}=p_\ell\,L_{\mathrm{km}}\,n_{\mathrm{lanes}}\,\min\!\big(1,\ f_{\min}+(1-f_{\min})(1-D(t))+c_q\,q(t)\big)\), with \(D(t)\) a smooth daylight indicator from seasonal sunrise and sunset, and \((p_\ell,c_q,f_{\min})\) per technology (LED adaptive: 16 kW/km/lane, 0.18, 0.20)
Ventilation
\(P_{\mathrm{vent}}=p_v\,L_{\mathrm{km}}\,n_{\mathrm{tubes}}\,\big(0.15+s\,q(t)\big)\,a\,g\,\big(1+s_p\,\mathbb 1_{\mathrm{pollution}}(t)+s_a\,\mathbb 1_{\mathrm{accident}}(t)\big)\), with \(p_v\) per system (longitudinal: 120 kW/km/tube), altitude factor \(a=1+\max(z-500,0)/6000\) and slope factor \(g=1+|i|/20\)
Auxiliaries
\(P_{\mathrm{aux}}=p_a\,L_{\mathrm{km}}\,n_{\mathrm{tubes}}\,(1+\min(z_{\max},800)/6000)\,(1+\eta_t)\), \(\eta_t\sim\mathcal N(0,0.025^2)\)
Events
pollution episodes and accidents drawn each day with given probabilities, start times and durations
How the load is built: one weekday, one realization, of the public example. PDF
Monte Carlo and indicators
\(R\) independent realizations (seeds \(42,43,\dots\)) give distributions of every indicator; the envelope reports the median and the P10–P90 band. P10 is the value below which 10% of the realizations fall, P90 the value below which 90% fall, and the median (P50) splits them into two halves: the P10–P90 band therefore holds the central 80%. Annual energy \(E=\sum_t P(t)\,\Delta t\); load factor \(\bar P/P_{\max}\); specific consumption \(E/\text{length}\).
Assumptions and validity
A first-order synthetic generator: the coefficients are engineering orders of magnitude, not measurements. Suitable for prototyping, teaching and pre-design sensitivity studies; calibrate against measured data before any engineering use.
Run it
The public example: a 1.5 km peri-urban tunnel, two tubes of two lanes, adaptive LED lighting, longitudinal ventilation, one year at 10 minutes, 20 realizations. The package lives in src/, hence PYTHONPATH=src. Executed on 22 October 2026 (Python 3.12).
git clone https://github.com/cyrilvoyant/tunnel-load-simulator.git
cd tunnel-load-simulator
pip install -r requirements.txt
PYTHONPATH=src python examples/monte_carlo_example.py # PowerShell: $env:PYTHONPATH="src"; python examples/monte_carlo_example.py
Output:
=== Monte Carlo results (20 runs) ===
Annual energy (MWh):
Median : 3233.4
P10 : 3229.5
P90 : 3237.1
Peak power (kW):
Median : 873.4
P10 : 792.2
P90 : 922.2
Other medians of the same run: mean power 369 kW, load factor 0.42, specific consumption 2,156 kWh per meter and year.
One week of the public example: median and P10–P90 band over 20 realizations. PDF
What you get
Annual energy (MWh), peak and mean power (kW), load factor, specific consumption (kWh/m/year) and event counts, for each run and as distributions.
Interactive charts and CSV export of the time series.
A Python package usable without the interface (run_monte_carlo(...)), with examples and tests.
Typical uses
Pre-design sensitivity studies: lighting technology, ventilation type, traffic level.
Synthetic load profiles for research on energy management and renewable integration in tunnels.
Teaching Monte Carlo uncertainty on an engineering case.
Status: first-order synthetic generator, suited to prototyping, demonstrations and pre-design sensitivity studies. Calibrate against measured data before any engineering or publication use.
SmartTunnel project and citation
Developed in the SmartTunnel research collaboration between Haytham El-Houari (Université Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah, Fès, Morocco) and Cyril Voyant (Mines Paris – PSL, O.I.E.). Cite the article: H. El-Houari, C. Voyant, Tunnel Load Simulator: a Monte Carlo framework for synthetic electrical demand modeling of road tunnels, SoftwareX 35, 102946, 2026, doi:10.1016/j.softx.2026.102946 · BibTeX; and the software: Tunnel Load Simulator, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20080042 (all versions).
Source code (MIT) · Also usable in plain language through WebSemantic.
